subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE ESTABLISHMENT OF CO-OPERATIVE EXTENSION SERVICE
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE ESTABLISHMENT OF CO-OPERATIVE EXTENSION SERVICE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should support the creation of a co-operative extension service, financed by Agriculture Canada, universities and provincial governments, for research and for the continuing education of farmers and extension personnel.
He said: Mr. Speaker, before I make some comments on this motion before the House in Private Members' Hour today, I would like to say, not that this is not an important subject, but I think there are other things that perhaps we could be discussing today. I want to point out to those who are watching the proceedings of the House today that this is part of the order of business of the House of Commons and so we will proceed with it.
It is a pleasure to rise to speak on the motion that I have before the House today. I will just read the motion again:
That, in the opinion of the House, the government should support the creation of a co-operative extension service, financed by Agriculture Canada, universities and provincial governments, for research and for the continuing education of farmers and extension personnel.
I want to speak for a just few minutes on this and to plead with the government to recognize the importance of the agriculture and the agrifood business in Canada. Since the election of this Parliament a little over two years ago, the Mulroney government has seemed to be going full speed ahead on deboning agricultural programs and taking away from primary producers and the agrifood industry many of the management tools and many of the programs that have been available to them in the past.

January 21, 1991
Private Members' Business
I recognize that agriculture is a joint jurisdiction between the federal government and the provincial governments, but I want to point out to them-and hopefully they will listen and recognize to a greater extent than they have indicated so far-the importance of the agrifood industry in this country. It is a $43 billion dollar industry. It employs one out of every five Canadians and, unless we take greater steps to replace or to change the programs that we have had taken away from the industry in the recent past, we are not going to be what we have to be; that is, competitive. That is the name of the game, whether in the agrifood industry or whatever other industry or business we are in. We must be competitive.
It is a false economy, a false view, and a false thinking if we do not give more emphasis to research and development in all industries, not only agriculture, and to continuing education for those not only at the primary producer level, but, as the motion reads, for extension service personnel level who work with primary producers and with agrifood industry people, on through the system.
The agricultural industry in this country, in the last couple of years more than ever, has come under a tremendous amount of pressure. It is not only the pressure that has been created by the free trade agreement. I maintained throughout that debate that the agrifood industry was going to be hit the hardest and the earliest of all industries that were going to be affected by the free trade agreement.
We can see what is happening there. We can see the rationalization taking place in our food processing industry. The cost to this country is that it is not making us as competitive as we should be because of the change in the rules that the free trade agreement put in place against the wishes and the advice of many of us who have a pretty good knowledge of how that industry operates, can operate, and should operate. In spite of all those recommendations, those rules were put in place and now we are paying the fiddler for the tune that was called and dictated to them.
I will cite an example that is very close. It is in my own riding. Just 10 days ago, another food processor announced that it was going to cease the growing and processing of vegetables. That is going to affect the farm-gate return of 25 producers in my riding to the tune
of $1.3 million per year. As well, it is going to eliminate over 150 seasonal jobs from the early part of February until the early part of November.
We cannot blame the people who are doing it. The bottom righthand comer in their balance sheet obviously dictates that they have to do that, but it is a rationalization. Now that the rules are changed, they are having to play with different rules, to deal with different tariff levels, et cetera.
This has been dictated by not only the free trade agreement, but other changes, as well. The rate of interest. The government will stand up and say: "The interest rate is not as high as it was a few years ago." I admit it is not as high as it was a few years ago, but the spread in the real interest rate between Canada and the United States is much higher than it was a few years ago.
In the last round of high interest rates, we were looking at around 2 per cent spread between Canada and the United States. Our businesses were far more competitive in that line than they are now. Now, as we all know, it is 4 or 5 per cent. It matters, yes, what the interest rate is, but what matters even more is the difference between Canada and the United States.
The high dollar. The dollar is being held up, and that puts it at an unreasonably high level. It makes the export capabilities of the whole agrifood industry much more difficult. We know what that is doing.
The other uncertainty that our industry is faced with at the present time is the uncertainty of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, the GATT talks which to date have not been successful.
As I have stated many times, I have very grave concerns that because of the way the GATT situation is going, not enough will be done in the agrifood industry and in trade and agricultural commodities throughout the world to do the job. If we are not able to get a successful conclusion there, I will feel very sorry for many, if not all, of our primary producers in the agrifood industry. That will certainly filter all the way up. What we have to remember and what the government has to remember is that if we do not have a healthy primary producer level, we will not have the production for the rest of the agrifood industry to work from and to work with.
It is very easy to say, as some people say, yes it is cheaper to buy food some place else in the world at the
January 21, 1991

present time, and I agree. In the short run, it would be. But what we have to consider and what I plead with the government to consider is to put those programs in place, put the dollars in place, and put the assistance in place in co-operation to a greater extent with the provinces. This will enable us to provide in the long run the food requirements and a sound agricultural and agrifood industry for Canadians.
In the short run, with many things in our lives we might gain, but we have to think further down the road than the present government is apparently thinking.
Not only does the agrifood industry supply to Canadians a source of food, it also supplies to Canadians the safest source of food of any population in the world. The agrifood industry not only provides that food source but reaches a lot of other goals and purposes in Canada. I do not feel that the present government has recognized that and is recognizing that to the extent that it should. Not only as I say does it provide a source of food, it provides a source of quality food. How better can we provide to Canadians and guarantee to Canadians that we are going to have a safe source of food for our children and our grandchildren down the road than to have that food produced under our own eyes in Canada as much as possible? We cannot produce all the commodities we wish, we know that. We do not have the climate. But we have to produce that under our own eyes, with our own rules, in our own yard, in our own country. It has to take place.
That will not take place unless there is economic sustainability. We talk about sustainable agriculture, we talk about the sustainable environment and I agree 100 per cent with all of those. What we have to realize is that unless financially the bottom right-hand comer of the balance sheet of an individual operation, an agrifood operation, or a processing operation, whatever it is, is in the black it cannot happen, and it will not happen as much as we all may believe within our hearts that it should happen and it is the right thing to do. It has to make financial sense.
If that is the case, I think that the priority of the importance of the agrifood industry should be higher than it is and should be realized by Canadians. Not only does it provide a safe, sound source of quality food, it
Private Members' Business
also provides and plays a role in the environment. Agriculture producers know better than anyone else, especially the primary producers, the role that they can play in the production of different crops, in soil conservation, water conservation, and wind erosion. That is another important role that we must realize the agrifood business plays.
It also plays a very major role in the balance of trade of this nation. It also plays a very major role in employment. One in five Canadians is employed in the agrifood industry. We do not need those people any place else. If we needed them some place else, I guess one could flippantly say: "Well, we'll take one out of those or we will take 20 per cent of them because we need them some place else in our economy. We do not need them." Heaven knows this government has created a situation and we have enough unemployment now.
There is another role that one might say is an intangible role that the agrifood industry plays and that is in the social fabric or fibre of this country. I had an opportunity this summer to take a couple of trips through the prairies. My 20-year old son was with me and he could not believe it. He said: "Dad, look what is happening to these towns". We have all seen the movies where they are boarding up the windows. And they were, Mr. Speaker. There are towns in western Canada where 4 four by eight sheets of plywood are put over 40 per cent, 50 per cent, or 60 per cent of the businesses in the town.
I do not really think the direction that we want to send the rural people in this country is to the bigger urban centres. Yes, the big urban centres can play a role, and do play a role, but I do not think that we need to chase people there any further.
They are being forced to go there in order to find another source of income so that they can continue to farm and in their view, and in the view of many of us, to provide Canadians with cheap food. I have nothing against cheap food, but we cannot produce cheap food on the backs of a big percentage of our population. It just cannot be done that way.
I am just warning Canadians and this government that if they continue along this line they are going to create a bad situation down the road. We have rightfully become

January 21, 1991
Private Members' Business
concerned about our environment for our children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren. We want them to have clean air and clean water.
What I am saying is we are going to have to put more programs in place in order to provide for our children, our grandchildren and our great-grandchildren. We must provide safe, quality, wholesome food that is produced here by a big sector of our economy.
We must remember that there are only four creators of wealth in the world, no matter what we look at, see, touch or use. Those four are fishing, mining, forestry and agriculture. This government is allowing many of these to falter.
We do not have to take time here to talk about the condition of our mining, lumbering and fishing. We know that they are in a deplorable economic situation. As well, it is creating social situations in Canada that are far from what we would like to have and have grown accustomed to. Agriculture is one of those.
As I have said, and many others have said, as goes agriculture, so goes the economy of any country. We could use as an example what has happened to Mr. Gorbachev. For a number of years he thought the war machine would fuel his economy. He has found out recently that the war machine does not fuel the economy because he has now has many millions of people who have empty stomachs, no food on the shelves and no place to get it.
What fuels a healthy, productive, efficient economy is full stomachs. Then people will be able to work and be able to produce for the good of all. We know that in the U.S.S.R. right now many people do not know how they are going to get through to the spring and through the next year. There is just not any food in the pantry, shelves or in the stomachs.
I want to remind the government of some of its own figures. The total receipts at the primary producer level for farm income in Canada is predicted in 1991 to be 4 per cent less than it was in 1990. That is 7 per cent less than it was in 1989.1 remind this House, Canadians and the government that no industry can continue when the receipts are going down.
We all know what it costs to do business and what it costs to live on an individual or business basis. The expenses are going up. The receipts are going down in an industry that has never been all that healthy. We just
cannot allow that to go on. If we allow that to go on in the short run, we are going to pay very dearly as Canadians in the long run.
There is a lot of stress and a lot of uncertainty in the agriculture community today because of some of the things that are happening, as I have said.
What I am encouraging the government to do is to work with some groups that are out there that are asking through the provincial governments and directly to the federal government for some financial assistance and, in some cases, the continuation of financial assistance.
The government has not assured these organizations that it will provide for yet another year, in order to put the extension personnel in the field to deal with the management and production stress that is there. In many farm families where the husband and wife are having to work off the farm, or at least one of them has to work off the farm, in a rural community it is not easy to get babysitters or whatever for child care.
I remind the government of a couple of programs that I would recommend it consider highly. There are two examples from Ontario. I feel that these examples throughout the country can serve a very useful purpose. One is the Advanced Agricultural Leadership Program that I am proud to say I was a part of getting established in Ontario a number of years ago. This program was one where farm, agrifood and extension people worked together on a two-year program in order to train people to meet the challenge for future leaders in dealing with provincial, national and international affairs, and to familiarize themselves of the needs of society and able to change rural Canada-and most of these are from Ontario-with a broad perspective. I recommend that the federal government do something through some department There have been applications to different ones and they have been turned down every time.
The other program is the Ontario Agricultural Training Institute. That is a program that is carried out by non-profit sectors. It is funded by 25 per cent of the individuals who participate in it and it is has helped put in place self-help training initiatives devoted to farmers and managing change. The major funding from this has been from employment and immigration. Unless it has happened in the last day or two, the federal government has refused, to this day, to approve funding for that program for another year.
January 21, 1991

I hope when my hon. colleagues reply today that they can give this House some good news in that they will announce that that funding is going to be put in place for next year because those are the types of co-operative programs that we need to continue.
In closing, I would like to remind the government of the importance and necessity of these types of programs so that we can strengthen our agrifood industry in this country so that we do not go behind at the rate we are going behind right now. I encourage and plead with the government to do so.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE ESTABLISHMENT OF CO-OPERATIVE EXTENSION SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to join in this debate.
As a former researcher who was heavily involved in extension and technology transfer, I know first-hand the importance of this issue to the agricultural industry. I am going to take a completely different approach in addressing this motion than the previous speaker has taken.
It is true that we are in a recession. It is true that it is having a significant effect on the agricultural industry. Apart from the approach taken by the previous speaker where he was wringing his hands about the future of the whole agricultural industry in Canada, certainly the future here looks as bright as in any country around the world.
He said that the government was de-boning agricultural policy and funding here in Canada. Any quick analysis of the expansion of funding since 1984 will clearly indicate that that simply is not true. With the recent announcements of the two new programs, GRIP and NISA, the government has committed itself to long-term programs in Canada which are certainly the most significant ever created in this country and are being very favourably received in the agricultural community.
When we look around the agricultural industry and the effects that current rationalization is having in that industry, it does cause some immediate concern.
When we look at what is happening on a world-wide scale, we see the world moving rapidly to freer trade everywhere, and very clearly consumers want that. The Canadian industry cannot survive with inefficient plants.
Private Members' Business
Instead of listening to and reading the negative headlines in the media and the newspapers every day, if we look at the business plans of Canadian industry in agriculture, particularly in agrifood processing, we will find that the number of new investments, expansions, and new plants in the food processing area in Canada are increasing very significantly. At last count, from January 1, 1989 to November 30, 1990 there were 30 new investments, 17 mergers, 39 plant closures, 50 new plants created, and 54 plant expansions. Every time there is a closure there are big headlines. Any time there is a new investment we have to look on page 43 of the business section to find it. Very clearly, the trend is to a much stronger and expanded food processing sector in Canada.
Everyone who happened to watch Venture on CBC a week ago Sunday night will have heard a number of food processing executives talking about the rationalization of Canada and the very positive future that particular industry has here.
Looking into the future and not wringing our hands about the immediate situation, although I do not want to minimize that because it is quite important and the agricultural sector needs help to get past it, how do we position farmers and the whole agricultural sector, which is so important to our economy? How do we position that to take advantage of the opportunities that will clearly exist in the next few years?
The government set up as part of the agrifood policy review last year the farm finance and management task force. All facets of the agrifood industry, including producers, worked with both levels of government to determine a long-term path to an economically stable farm community. The importance of improving farm profitability and performance through improved management research and extension efforts was central to the focus of that task force.
In its June report to the federal and provincial ministers of agriculture, the task force recommended the development of a national program in farm management training services and information. This would involve industry, both levels of government, and post-secondary schools of all types.
At their August meeting in Moncton, the ministers accepted the recommendation for the development of a national program. Going one step further, they set up a govemment/industry working group to draft proposals

Private Members' Business
for implementing such a program. A final report is expected at the end of April.
In an increasingly competitive global market, it is important that farmers have access to the up-to-date technology information they need to manage their farms effectively. The task force pointed out that governments alone were not capable of ensuring a complete flow of information to producers. That is why it is strongly suggested co-operation between members involved in the whole food chain, to make this whole approach quite efficient, wide-ranging, and to get all the information services out there to all parts of the agrifood industry.
The task force suggested the establishment of a long-term program for farm management. Federal and provincial governments and industry would co-operate and co-ordinate the program on a national basis so it could be delivered regionally to ensure individual needs are met. Regional delivery is quite important because of the various crops, climates, soil types, and so on across this country.
Specifically the task force proposed that the farm management program offer three levels of service to producers, the first being training and development services. This would include the development of modular training packages, curriculum, and so on. The second is to offer management services, which of course are very important to producers. Third, the program would offer information services and improvement over what is already offered among the extension services in existence already in Canada, which by the way are quite good.
This is a wide-ranging program involving both levels of government, colleges, universities, farm organizations, private sector lenders, and consultants all working together to co-operate and finance this organization.
We believe that changes in existing structures will handle the challenges in the future, that we do not need a completely new extension service. We just need to adapt the old one, which has developed as the needs of Canada have affected its development. We need just a bit more fine tuning and co-operation so that we can get the information out to our industry and position it very favourably to meet the challenges of the future.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE ESTABLISHMENT OF CO-OPERATIVE EXTENSION SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in this debate today, although, like the mover of the motion, the member for Prince Edward-Hastings said, it is perhaps unusual for us to be debating a motion like this in times of national crisis. It is true also that life continues and other issues are still there for us to deal with.
Certainly one of those issues is the crisis which faces rural Canada today, in particular the agricultural community. It would be a mistake to let that focus be forgotten. Therefore, I am happy that this private member's motion is before us today.
There is no question that we are at a turning point when it comes to the future of agriculture and rural communities in our country. The process of centralization, the process of decline, has gone on for long enough. It has become incremental, in that it is operating at an accelerating pace. The percentage of farmers leaving is rapidly increasing. The percentage of farmers in trouble and that impact on the rural community is increasing at an incremental rate.
Therefore it becomes more and more urgent that action be taken. We can no longer feel that we have the time to deal with this matters on a gradual basis or on a long-term basis. Many of these issues need to be addressed now.
Certainly I accept the fact, as the member pointed out, that we are dealing with a primary industry in this country which employs 20 per cent of Canadians. One in five is dependent on the agricultural industry. We are dealing with food, the most basic of human needs which the world cannot do without. We also have to consider that one-third of Canadians, in spite of what has happened to rural Canada, still lives in rural Canada. Their future, the future of their children, and the future of their community depend very much on the direction in which we head.
The pressures we are under are quite self-evident. We have pressures that flow from the free trade deal. It opens up our way of handling our agricultural industry and our processing industry to harmonization with the approach of Americans. The American market is much larger. There are much larger economies of scale. I think there is much less emphasis on farm based institutions

and much less emphasis on support for the family farm. This is placing our agricultural industry, our farmers, under increasing pressure as this process becomes more advanced.
There is the whole international situation which was clearly focused in the GATT where there are real international differences on how we should approach this matter. On the one hand, the Europeans feel, because of their history and their geography and the fact that they starved during the war and because they have a very small area and do not want their cities any more crowded, that it is worth their while to keep as many farmers on the land as possible. They are prepared to pay the price to do so.
On the other hand, the United States feels, with its treasury and with its huge economies of scale, that it can blast anybody it wants to out of the market and is prepared to do so, using public moneys. Often forgotten is the fact that throughout the Third World the majority of people are still engaged in agriculture. While this whole trade war is affecting us in many dire ways, it is even more devastating to the farmers in the Third World who already live very marginal lives and have very marginal enterprises. They are being devastated by the whole situation.
A third pressure comes from the evolving awareness of what we are doing to our environment and the whole movement toward sustainable agriculture. This is going to force upon the farm community, if the farm community does not itself willingly adopt some of these perspectives, a whole new way of looking at agriculture, a whole new way of managing its affairs, with things like what kind of chemicals we use, how we handle our livestock, pesticides, herbicides, and so on. These matters will all be affected very much by the way this environmental debate unfolds in this country. It is going to create another whole set of factors to which the farm community will have to adapt in the years to come. If the rural community is not itself actively engaged in this debate, that debate is going to be forced upon it.
We have the' centralizing forces, which are perhaps part of the larger scheme of things and very much either a conscious or a subconscious part of government policy. I think this is outlined very well in the recent book by the hon. member for Edmonton Southeast wherein he
Private Members' Business
outlines very convincingly that both Liberal and Conservative governments in this country over the last 20 to 25 years have poured immense resources and developmental energies into the urban centres, very much to the neglect of the outlying regions or outer Canada, as he describes it. Inner Canada has had all the attention, all the resources, and all the investment, while outer Canada where one-third of Canadians live has been very much on the short end of the stick. Historical trends have been exacerbated even more by deliberate policy decisions of government through the years.
This has certainly led us to our current crisis. As the member for Prince Edward-Hastings said in his remarks, national cash income is expected to fall 4 per cent in Canada. It is 9 per cent in Saskatchewan this year. This means a 37 per cent drop in net income in Canada and a 60 per cent drop in net income in Saskatchewan. If we look at Saskatchewan's net income, there was already only a $5,000 a year income from farming sources for Saskatchewan farm families. If we take away 60 per cent of $5,000, we are left with a $2,000 income per farm family from farming operations. Surely that is a total disaster. It needs to be dealt with, not at some time in the future, not even as soon as our new safety net programs are expected to kick in, but on a very immediate basis.
It is also incumbent on us to present some alternatives.
That is why I am happy the proposal has been made. I was at Michigan State University, which is a land grant university in the United States, where the whole concept of co-operative education was pioneered. There it is understood that the partnership is among industry, the state, the local levels of government and the university. The universities essentially run the program.
I was very intrigued by that, because in Canada it is quite different. Here it is government which runs extension services. Originally, when I observed it, I felt that it was perhaps more appropriate to keep it running out of government agencies. Since then, I have noted a few things. One is the politicization of agriculture services in my home province of Saskatchewan by the Devine government where his support very much depends on his rural base. He uses the agriculture extension services to underpin that base.
Second, the massive need for change which has come upon the farm community over the last 10 years tells me

Private Members' Business
it is very important that we develop the kind of co-operative model which the member is talking about.
I support the proposal. As well, I support a movement toward safety net programs which are geared to the cost of production formulas. These should be the centrepiece of farm support programs.
We also have to deal with the question of farm debt. We cannot leave that to the free market. We need to deal with farm debt on an urgent basis. The way we are doing it now is leaving this generation, future generations and in fact past generations of farmers sinking under the weight of their debt load.
We need to deal with the infrastructure and rural development on a wider basis. We have to support farmer institutions which have allowed Canada to develop a unique role in agriculture that supports family farmers and their institutions like the Wheat Board, the wheat pools and marketing boards.
In closing, I might also refer to the platform of another party that only has one member in this House and therefore little opportunity to put views on the record. The Reform Party of Canada, by contrast, calls for a shift from government domination to an industry shaped by market forces. It pushes for an extension of free trade agreements with the United States to include common internal export subsidy arrangements.
It calls for the removal of the Crow rate through a one-time non-taxable bridge payment. It calls for the anti-eastern feed freight assistance and a re-orientation of the Farm Credit Corporation on a commercial basis, for future privatization and for the reduction of farm marketing boards as a cost-saving measure.
I am pleased to be able to put my views on the record to support the proposal of the hon. member. Rural Canada has been in retreat long enough. It is time to move forward. I would urge all members of Parliament to look for every way they can to assist the farm community in facing the challenges of the future.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE ESTABLISHMENT OF CO-OPERATIVE EXTENSION SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to address this motion that has been put forward by the hon. member opposite from Prince Edward-Hastings. The motion states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should support
the creation of a co-operative extension service, financed by
Agriculture Canada, universities and provincial governments, for
research and for the continuing education of farmers and extension
personnel.
This certainly sounds all very correct, something that everyone should be supporting.
I would like to put on the record some of the things that are taking place. There can be no doubt as to the need for continuing research and education in our rapidly changing world. Farmers are not immune to changes, and their information needs continue to grow as well. The critical step is the efficient delivery of information to those who need it, and in a manner which can be readily put to use.
The motion before us today appears to imply that we need to completely overhaul an already existing structure, the authority for which lies within provincial jurisdiction. Before we jump into this unknown area, perhaps we should review our current situation.
If the member is implying that we should duplicate the system in place in the United States, there are several factors that need to be clarified. As hon. members may know, the U.S. system is a joint federal-state-university service.
First, what will be the cost? No doubt it would be rather substantial, particularly during the transition period to a new system.
Second, what would be the impact on Canadians who are currently involved in research and extension service delivery?
Third, is such a system relevant to today's reality? While it has been successful in the past, many of the more educated American farmers are questioning whether such a system best serves their needs.
This government favours an alternate approach that would encourage a more co-operative, responsible and effective extensive service which builds upon the institutional structures already in place across Canada.
As hon. members know, under our federal system, responsibility and authority for various aspects of Canadian agriculture are shared between the federal and provincial levels of government. This sharing of responsibility and authority is based not just on the Constitution Act but also on historical and traditional practices that have evolved over time.

Today, the federal government carries the principal responsibility for agrifood related research. Some provinces also support active research programs which have helped broaden our knowledge base. In my own riding, at the research station at Agassiz, which has been there for over 100 years, there is co-operation between industry and the research station. The industries put several thousands of dollars every year into the agriculture base so that research can take place next door to where the industry is operating. That is mainly concerning some of the supply managed commodities. This also applies to the horticulture areas. They are experimenting with various crops that can be grown in the Fraser Valley. These things are ongoing and in place at present.
In recent years, there has been a move toward greater private sector involvement in agriculture food research. The result has been an increase in federal-provincial-private sector co-operation and in research activities. This is ongoing and I applaud it.
The provincial governments have the primary responsibility for extension services but the federal government has been involved in a limited and measured way. Examples of this involvement include federal-provincial development agreements, direct technology transfers through Agriculture Canada's research branch and the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration-which was better known when I grew up as the PFRA-and farm finance and management services through the Farm Credit Corporation and farm management specialists and agricultural economists.
Universities and colleges in Canada undertake a variety of agricultural research and extension activities. The level of effort varies substantially across institutions and provinces depending most often on the importance of agriculture to the regional and local economy.
This is one of the fundamental strengths of the current separation of responsibility as exists in Canada. While a national program may, at first glance, seem like the best way to go, more often than not, it is the local and regional interests that are in the best position to determine local needs.
Recognizing this regional diversity and growing importance of a more self-reliant, market responsive and environmentally sustainable agrifood industry in Canada, the Minister of Agriculture launched a comprehen-
Private Members' Business
sive review of Canada's agrifood policy in December of 1989.
Since that time, 11 task forces and committees have been examining a range of agrifood issues and have provided advice on possible future actions. The minister and his provincial colleagues have met to discuss these recommendations on two occasions, and a third meeting is anticipated soon.
One of the 11 committees has been examining research and technology transfer issues. In fact, in conjunction with the Canadian Agriculture Research Council, a national conference on research and technology transfer priorities will be held in June of this year. Stakeholders from across the whole spectrum of the agrifood sector will be involved.
To highlight the co-operation that is being reinforced by the policy review, the provinces have agreed that Agriculture Canada will focus on the delivery of technology and information to provincial specialists who, in turn, will pass it along to producers.
Agriculture Canada, through the recently established Industry Relations Office, is also working closing with the private sector on the commercialization of technologies developed by the department. The task force on competitiveness confirmed the importance of effective technology transfer for a healthy and competitive agrifood industry. At their meeting in Winnipeg last November, agriculture ministers agreed to participate in the creation of an industry-led agrifood competitiveness council that will serve as a catalyst in turning task force recommendations into action.
Another task force has looked at farm finance and farm management issues. This past August in Moncton, federal and provincial agriculture ministers accepted the four recommendations of the task force. Those recommendations include the need to develop a national farm policy; to establish a clearly defined role for the Farm Credit Corporation; to extend the mandate of the farm debt review boards; and to establish a national program for farm management training services and information.
Now that the task force reports are in, the next few months will be dedicated to putting concrete measures into place that will meet the policy needs of Canadian farmers.

January 21, 1991
So you see, Mr. Speaker, the government is well aware of the need to provide effective extension services to Canadian farmers, whether it be in the research technology transfer or farm management training.
As has been the practice of this government since 1984, we are moving forward by consulting with our provincial colleagues, industry and producers.
The intended results of our efforts is not to substantially change the existing institutions or to build new ones simply to provide an illusion of action. The intended result is a more co-operative, responsive and effective extension service for Canadian farmers.
In closing, I would like to say that the various programs that I see first hand at the Agassiz Research Station and the field days that they conduct and the involvement of the farm community is just another example of the co-operation that goes on between the industry and the research stations in agriculture in Canada.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE ESTABLISHMENT OF CO-OPERATIVE EXTENSION SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have an opportunity, if only for a couple of moments, to speak to the motion of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings this afternoon because it deals with the whole range of government support programs, extension, research and so on.
I had the opportunity in 1987 or 1988 to visit most of the research facilities across Canada and to see how important they are to Canadian farm producers and in many cases how the co-operation between the federal and provincial governments provides these services, especially in Kentville, Nova Scotia, Lethbridge, Alberta and many other places across the country.
In the couple of moments that we have available to us, I would like to point out how devastating the figures are which the government released just last week. They show that in 1991 net farm income will be reduced by some 54.5 per cent from 1990, and 1990 was not a particularly good year in itself. Obviously, net farm income was twice as high as it will be in 1991.
Much of this reduction in net farm income-we hear that the Manitoba farm income will plummet by 51 per cent and other provinces likewise is due to the government's incessant reduction in government support programs since the 1988 general election. From 1988 to 1989 the reduction was over $100 million; in 1989 to 1990 some $1.3 billion; and in 1991 it is projected to be
reduced another $400 million. We face a dramatic and plummeting reduction in government support programs which likewise is reducing net farm income, as I said, in 1991 by some 54 per cent, from $4.3 billion to $1.9 billion.
This motion deals with the matter of research and development. In the government's support programs for agriculture research in 1986 to 1990 in constant dollars there is a reduction of some $4 million in operating budgets. Capital budgets have been slashed by $15 million, transfer payments by some $500 million, and the total reduction is almost $20 million.
Thus, in the budget of 1989, the government really started to lower the boom on Canadian agriculture producers and has been doing so ever since. This is a time when world grain prices are the lowest in history. The demand and marketing is at the lowest in history. It is simply unconscionable.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday night during the debate on the war against Iraq, over 200 people phoned the opposition lobby to talk to members of Parliament involved in that debate.
Only three of these callers supported the government position of using Canadian fighter aircraft against Iraq. The other 200 callers completely and vigorously opposed the government's position in this war. Many of the callers said they could not sleep. In fact, they had not been able to sleep since the war began.
I would like to place some of the comments on the record and share them with you. One of the callers said: "This war is a tremendous error." Another said: "It is totally reckless." Another caller said: "Bring our forces back. They have no business in that war." Another caller
January 21, 1991

said: "We are ashamed of our government in terms of what it has done."
One of the most poignant calls was from Will Williams, a 100 per cent disabled Vietnam veteran from DeForest, Wisconsin. He was sickened by what George Bush has done and by the Congress for supporting him. He urged us to continue fighting against this war, a war created by George Bush.
Other colleagues will place more of these comments on the record today.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the world's concern has been focused on the war in the gulf, attention has been diverted from the tragic events in the Baltic states. The recent attacks by the Soviet army on the people of the Baltic republics of Lithuania and Latvia are clearly as unacceptable as the aggressive acts of Saddam Hussein.
The unfolding of events in the Baltics and the gulf are frighteningly similar to those in 1956, when the Soviet army invaded Hungary while the world was occupied with the Suez crisis. With that in mind, the Soviet Union must immediately take concrete steps to ensure that aggression such as we have seen in Lithuania last week and Latvia on the weekend is not repeated.
Canada must condemn the actions of the Soviet army by petitioning the United Nations to address these obvious violations of basic human rights and to support the right to self-determination. Canada should also seriously reconsider its aid to the Soviet Union in light of recent events.
It is tragically ironic that, as a signatory of the UN resolutions condemning Iraq, the Soviet Union must now seek to repair its own violations of the UN charter.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again the government has violated international law in its treatment of Canada's aboriginal people.
The Canadian Centre of International Pen, in co-operation with the Faculty of Law at the University of Toronto, undertook a study of Canada's obligations to native people under international law in response to the 1990-1991 federal budget cuts to native communication programs.
The government's treatment of aboriginal people will now be discussed by the United Nations Commission on Human Rights in Geneva.
I commend the Pen organization and the University of Toronto for their initiative and their interest. As the PEN president, John Ralston Saul, stated this morning: "This budget cut isn't a large one, just a small surgically-precise incision, enough to cut out the voice box of the native people."
The federal government wants to deny native people the very fundamental right of the freedom of speech.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday I read for the first time Amnesty International's detailed report of human rights violations committed in Kuwait before the war.
Amnesty International asked the Iraqi government, after it had released several hundred western nationals, to end the imprisonment, torture and killings of several thousand people in Kuwait. We were shocked and horrified by the torture methods used by the Iraqi forces.
The team of investigators listed the names of about
1,000	people who had been arrested but believes the exact number is much higher. Thousands of people, including 13 year olds, are still being held in Iraqi and Kuwaiti prisons, detention centres and private homes. Others were killed shortly after their arrest at police stations or at their homes, or were gunned down.
Mr. Speaker, we all join Amnesty International in asking for a stop to the torture and killing in Kuwait by the Iraqis.

January 21, 1991

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his comments on the Persian Gulf war, the Prime Minister has enjoyed quoting past Prime Ministers in similar situations. I would like to take this opportunity to quote some of the comments of average Canadians who called the House of Commons during the all-night debate early Saturday morning, January 19, 1991.
A Burnaby caller asked: "How do we change our role from peacekeepers to war-makers?"
A Newfoundland caller stated that "innocent women, children, and old people in Kuwait and Iraq did not cause this war, yet they are going to get hurt and killed".
Another caller told us that "people think this is one big Nintendo game. These are live players. It is not an artificial thing that gets eradicated. It is live flesh and blood."
From New Brunswick came: "Please continue to oppose this resolution. No one with 14 per cent public support has the mandate to take a country to war."
A Toronto caller said: "I came to Canada because I thought it was a safe haven. The actions of this government have destroyed that."
Another caller told us: "It is never too late to make a change to Canada's policy and turn Canada into a peacekeeper."
The Prime Minister should be more concerned with the opinions of ordinary Canadians, rather than quoting past politicians.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to talk about the total failure of federal fisheries policies in southwest Nova Scotia.
The minister has made much of the Hache task force as a basis of his groundfish management program. But I attended those meetings and hearings and none of the inshore fishermen I met there backed the department's new ideas. In fact, there has been a lack of agreement.
We now have the individual transferable quota system which gives experienced fishermen ridiculously low quotas. Some fishermen are so angry at the new system that they are taking the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to court to solve it.
Because of the enterprise allocation to the offshore, National Sea Products is now renting these inshore boats to fish quota that used to go to these inshore communities.
Since December 18, 1990, I have been asking the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans for a meeting to discuss the situation, with no reply. I call on the minister to meet with me and, if not me, at least local fishermen to seek a reasonable solution quickly before things get out of hand.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on August 2 the world watched with dismay as Iraq declared war and invaded Kuwait. The United Nations was quick to state its opposition to dictator Saddam Hussein's aggression. Canada actively participated in UN sanctions against Iraq. While months went by, many diplomatic solutions were sought. Saddam Hussein continued to say no to all peace initiatives.
On January 15, the allied forces, some 30 nations strong, moved to free Kuwait.
I call on all political parties to support Canada and the United Nations war effort, and on all Canadians to unite in our support of the men and women in the Canadian Armed Forces. We pray for their safety.
The nations of the world must find a lasting peace in the Middle East and throughout the world.
speakername: Mr. Walter Van  De Walle@St. Albert

speakerposition: subtopic
Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hundreds of Canadians phoned the House of Commons opposition lobby early Saturday morning to let NDP MPs know how they feel about Canada's participation in the gulf war. Here are some of their comments.
A World War II veteran sarcastically complimented the Prime Minister for getting us into this mess. Another, a veteran of both World War II and the Korean War and a member of my father's regiment-the Queen's
January 21, 1991

Own Cameron Highlanders of Winnipeg-said that the only common sense being heard in the House of Commons is from those who oppose the war.
A current member of the Canadian forces called to say that Canada's forces are ill-equipped to do what they are attempting to do, but that Canada is perfectly equipped for a peacekeeping role.
A woman from Nanaimo pointed out that she had lived in Britain through World War II and is against this war. "We should not bomb other people," she said.
Finally, a comment that sums up the feelings of many who called: "Please continue to oppose the resolution. No one with 14 per cent public support has the mandate to take the country to war."
At least one party is prepared to listen to the voices of reason from one end of this country to the other. I am proud to be a New Democrat.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Iraq has not only rejected outright countless peace initiatives, but used the pause for peace to consolidate its grip over a sovereign nation taken by force and held under terror.
It is evident to all the world that the aggressor has no interest in discussion, negotiation or diplomacy. History has shown that appeasement does not work. Regrettably the world community had no alternative but to take the steps necessary to preserve world order and to safeguard the effectiveness and indeed the very future of the United Nations. Peace has a price. Canada now, as in the past, is prepared to meet that price.
I pay tribute to the men and women of the Canadian Armed Forces on duty in the gulf. They serve Canada in furtherance of UN resolution 678, not in a world as we would wish it to be, but in the real world. They are facing the grim reality of war and doing so with honour and
courage. These brave Canadians are defending the values and interests of Canada.
Our thoughts and prayers are with them and their families. They have our respect and gratitude.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, regardless of our views on the decision to engage our forces in battle, we must unite as Canadians in support of the men and women of our Armed Forces. They are bravely putting their lives at risk in the hope that this conflict will be resolved quickly and peace restored.
Nobody wants to see Canadian forces engaged in battle. We would have preferred a peaceful solution to this conflict. However, we are now in a state of war and we must be careful to ensure that the actions we take and the speeches that we make in the House do not in any way adversely affect the morale of our Armed Forces.
War is always a time of pain, trauma, and hardship. It is also a time for our country to pull together. In speaking with my constituents on this matter, I recognize that there exists some diverse views as to what our role in the Persian Gulf should be. But most would agree that our thoughts, prayers, and support must go out to the men and women of our Armed Forces.
Let us hope that their efforts are accomplished with a minimal loss of life and that they are soon on their way back home.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no Canadian seeks war, but we have a responsibility to protect the peace. The United Nations was founded to protect the world from unprovoked aggression. Canadians are willing to accept their responsibility to uphold the principles and mandate of the United Nations.
The son of the late Prime Minister Pearson, Geoffrey Pearson, was quoted this weekend as having said: "My father was no pacifist. His policy was based above all on the United Nations' importance as a peacekeeper. But

Oral Questions
once war broke out, he felt that UN member countries should use military intervention to oppose the aggressor."
He went on to say: "So, aside from a few slight differences, I think Mr. Clark is following Canada's diplomatic tradition."
Our nation is not a nation of pacifists. We are a nation of peacemakers. Today our forces are helping to establish peace in the Persian Gulf. Canadians did not want this war, but we are willing to accept our responsibility to uphold the principles and mandate of the United Nations.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is incumbent upon all of us to raise the morale any way possible for our troops in the multinational force.
It has long been a tradition to paint names and messages on the fronts of missiles to be launched, but I would like to suggest that our multinational forces no longer print Saddam on any missiles. No, Mr. Speaker, I would rather have them print Saddam in reverse, because Saddam spelled backwards is M-A-D-D A-S.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite intensive diplomatic effort prior to January 15, war has broken out and Canadians are trying to come to grips with it.
Violence is not an effective means of resolving disputes and we all wish it had not come to this.
We know it is difficult to imagine an end to this war but it will end one day and the issue will not be who wins or who loses, because, clearly, we all lose in situations like this. One of my constituents said: "Our world, poised on the brink of environmental collapse, crying out for the most basic reforms to bring some justice, food, and hope to the Third World, just cannot afford this waste of resources and lives."
Once this crisis is over, Canada and the United Nations will face a very important challenge and that is to find a long-lasting solution to the problems in the
Middle East. To this end, it is my hope that the day will come when words like "war", "violence", and "destruction" will be removed from the dictionary of humanity and replaced by "dialogue", "diplomacy", and "peace".

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, war is one of the least acceptable human behaviours but even less acceptable is not standing up for your beliefs when all possible diplomatic alternatives have been attempted and rejected.
On Friday, some 200 students gathered at the University of Calgary to express their support for the United Nations forces, including the Canadian Armed Forces, seeking lasting peace in the Persian Gulf region. In a statement that speaks for many in southern Alberta, a home-made sign was hung over Memorial Drive in Calgary. It said simply, and I quote: "Canadians with life experience support you, Brian. The peace we enjoy costs something".

January 21, 1991

allies which will deal with the problem definitively on the battle field.
As far as our commitment is concerned, this is something I mentioned before, which was also mentioned by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and it is an integral part of our Canadian policy.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister on another very serious international situation. As the Prime Minister knows, this past weekend, Soviet troops attacked the Latvian Department of the Interior, and at least five people were killed, some of whom were civilians and some of whom were press people. This crackdown came just one week after Soviet troops moved into Lithuania, killing 14 people. Will the government call in the ambassador of the U.S.S.R. and express to him the outrage of the people of Canada at this use of force?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are looking at action in three broad areas.
One, of course, is in our bilateral relations with the Soviet Union. We have indicated to them already that the line of credit and other emergency assistance that had been discussed by our government is under review.
The Leader of the Opposition will know that, even within the Canadian community of Baltic origins, there is some question as to whether or not we should be involved in actions that have to do with the delivery of foodstuffs to the Soviet Union. That is a matter that is being considered.
We are also looking at other actions on a bilateral basis that made it abundantly clear that this action by the Soviet Union will adversely affect relations between our two countries.
Second, we are looking at actions that can be taken internationally. There was a question raised by my colleague from Winnipeg and again by the member for Calgary the other day, and we are examining whether it is possible to raise these matters through the CSCE or through the United Nations. There is a problem of a Soviet de facto veto in both cases.
Finally, Canada is looking at concrete ways in which we can support the Baltic states through increased contacts and direct assistance. I hope to have the opportunity to discuss some of those in detail in my meeting later today.

Mr. Speaker, my questions are to the same minister.
As we know, one week ago, the world witnessed the bloody crackdown against Lithuania. Today, the Canadian Latvian community is outraged by the senseless tragedy of the Soviet black berets killing and maiming innocent civilians and journalists in Riga over the weekend.
I would like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs: In light of the critical events happening in the Baltic states, would he, which he can do pursuant to Standing Order 53, call for an emergency debate on this very critical issue?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would certainly favour an emergency debate by this House on that matter.
I believe that there may be the opportunity for that issue to be discussed among House leaders. Indeed, it may already be under consideration by House leaders, and I would not want to intrude upon their decisions.
I think it would be helpful following the unanimous resolution that was passed here if there were a short, clear debate by this Parliament allowing representative members of Parliament of all parts of the House to express their views clearly and unequivocally to the Soviet people and, indeed, to the people of the Baltic republics.

Mr. Speaker, to the same minister.
This Saturday, January 19, my colleague from Scarborough Centre and I attended a meeting with close to 500 Canadians of Baltic descent to discuss this current crisis in the Baltic states.
Among other demands, Baltic Canadians want the Government of Canada to call on the United Nations to send observers to the region and to recognize the councils of the republics in Canada. I want to ask the minister: Will he consider these two requests from the Baltic Canadians? Can we expect some action on these two recommendations as soon as possible?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Scarborough Centre, as is her custom on these matters, brought the contents of this discussion immediately to my attention this morning.
We had an opportunity to discuss it in detail. I am not yet in a position to respond to the question put in the House by my hon. friend and put to me earlier by the hon. member for Scarborough Centre, but we hope to be able to respond in-excuse me?
What is the U.S. doing?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member speaking from her seat asks what the United States is doing.
She would be interested to know that, among the communications to the Soviet Union by western leaders, no one spoke more strongly, no position was more
emphatically stated than that by the Prime Minister of Canada.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, indeed, without commenting upon her question or upon the reaction of other countries, I can say without any fear of contradiction that the statement by the Prime Minister of Canada was the strongest issued by any leader of a western government and we intend to follow in that course.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 25 of last year, one week before Saddam Hussein attacked Kuwait, the U.S. ambassador told him that she had been instructed by James Baker to say: "We have no opinion on the Arab-Arab conflicts like your border disagreement with Kuwait. The issue is not associated with America."
Given this history and given western and U.S.S.R. arms sales to Iraq, can the Prime Minister indicate whether Canada agreed with these early U.S. signals and with these arms sales to Iraq, and what concrete diplomatic efforts Canada is making, both at the United Nations and in direct dialogue, hopefully with Iraq and through the Arab league, to bring this mad war to an immediate end?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had extensive conversations with foreign ministers in the region and with Secretary-General Perez de Cuellar with regard to means by which this matter can be ended peacefully. I believe the hon. member knows that.
He will also know that Mr. Perez de Cuellar has expressed his view that there has to be a response by Saddam Hussein to the actions of the United Nations before there can be serious talk of a pause, a withdrawal or other actions of this kind. We agree with the Secretary-General of the United Nations on that matter.
I certainly did not know at the time what conversations ensued between the ambassador of another country and Iraqi authorities in July. Certainly it is our view that the questions raised by the invasion of Kuwait, that direct challenge to international law, and the refusal by Saddam Hussein to respect or respond to the wishes of the
January 21, 1991

world united, is a matter which raises direct Canadian interests and requires a Canadian response.

Mr. Speaker, of course, the minister has not dealt with the very important question of arms sales into that region in the period leading up to the invasion.
My supplementary question is for the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister knows that with the massive carpet bombing now under way in Iraq the objectives of this war are not, if they ever were, to solely remove Iraq from Kuwait in compliance with UN resolutions, but clearly to destroy Iraq militarily, economically and socially. In short, this is not a UN authorized war but a U.S. led war.
Will the Prime Minister now tell Canadians how many men, women and children have died in this war, both civilian and military, including the republican guard, since censorship denies us this fundamental information? Will the Prime Minister now recognize that Canadian troops should not be involved in this tragic war but instead, Canada should be playing a humanitarian, medical role and ultimately, a peacekeeping role, to help reduce the terrible toll that this war will take in human, economic and ecological terms?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think most of us in this House believe that the most humanitarian action that can be taken is to end this conflict quickly, to end it finally and to end it in a way that respects not only the integrity of Kuwait, but also the effectiveness of the United Nations. That is what we are trying to do. I have no idea what the hon. member is trying to do.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the right hon. Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister will know that an all-party delegation has just returned from the Horn of Africa which currently faces a famine of biblical portions. The gulf war is likely to seriously complicate the delivery of emergency relief through the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden to the Sudan and Eritrean ports.
Oral Questions
Would the Prime Minister therefore undertake to inform the United Nations and other relief agencies that Canada, if asked to do so, is prepared to redeploy our air and naval forces already in the gulf to provide escort services for the delivery of humanitarian aid to the Horn of Africa?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all the implications of that question will of course have to be looked at with some care.
My colleague, the Minister for International Trade, will be meeting with the all-party delegation which has just returned from the Horn of Africa. We are very concerned about the situation there and want to take practical steps to be of help to it.
The hon. member, inadvertently perhaps, underlines that when Saddam Hussein attacked Kuwait, when he started this war, he had effects not only upon the people of Kuwait, but he had effects upon suffering people everywhere in the world: in the Horn of Africa, in Zimbabwe, in Senegal, and in Bangladesh.
That is why this has to be stopped, and that is why it has to be stopped within the authority of the United Nations.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Today and tomorrow in Ottawa, the Department of External Affairs is meeting with various NGOs in the preparation of the upcoming 47th session of the UN Commission on Human Rights. The cruel and unwarranted human rights violation against the people of the Baltic states should be a top priority at this session.
Would the minister outline what steps Canada will take at this session on human rights to help bring an end to these atrocities in the Baltic states?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the consultations with non-governmental organizations interested in hu-

January 21, 1991
Oral Questions
man rights is precisely to ensure that we have the best advice from the non-governmental sector as to how we can advance legitimate Canadian interests most effectively through United Nations agencies.
There are people who are speaking on behalf of the Baltic peoples participating in those meetings. We will certainly take their advice seriously. If there are ways in which those interests can be advanced through the United Nations, we will advance them.
I make the point that we must also act on other fronts. That is why we are looking, in addition to the United Nations, to the CSCE; why the Prime Minister sent a very strong letter to Mr. Gorbachev; and why we are looking at other ways in which we can offer symbolic and substantial help to the Baltic peoples.

My supplementary question is directed to the same minister, Mr. Speaker.
These outrageous atrocities are happening today. They happened yesterday and they happened last week. Still I hear that we plan to keep moving at a slow pace.
Would the minister please assure me and the people on this side of the House that he has instructed these people who are meeting with the NGOs to try to attempt to bring an end to these gross violations of human rights? Would the minister please assure me that he has asked these people to make that representation?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very important that this House be heard. It is very important that individual members, like the hon. member who has spoken, stand and express their concerns as evocatively as they can. But, at the end of the day, these kinds of expressions of opinion by parliamentarians in Canada will be effective only if we can find resolute ways that persuade Soviet authorities.
That is why the Prime Minister of Canada deliberately sent the strongest message sent by any western leader to Mr. Gorbachev insisting that he desist. That is why we have made it clear that the nature of relations between Canada and the Soviet Union will be very much affected by his response to that position. That is why we are looking at ways that have not been developed before and that may not be acceptable to other countries by which we can establish symbolic and substantial help to the Baltic peoples.
The members words are welcome. If she has suggestions as to particular actions that will work, that will be effective, that will have a resonance beyond this House, I would welcome hearing from her.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Considering the tragic events in the Baltic states and the involvement of the Soviet army, will the minister stop the deportation of refugees from those countries, especially those who do not want to be drafted into the Soviet army?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have a deportation policy that is very sensitive to the situation in countries that are part of the Soviet Union. Similarly, people from the Soviet Union who are in this country may apply for a visa extension in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I have been informed this weekend that some refugees from the Baltic states presently in Canada are being deported. They believe that once they are in the Soviet Union they will be drafted by the army.
Will the minister make sure there is no deportation into the Baltic states?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been very sensitive to the situation in the Baltic states. Of course the people from these states carry Soviet passports, so it is up to them to identify themselves as being from a Baltic state.
However, our practices will continue to be very sensitive to the situation there.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It also pertains to the situation in Latvia and Lithuania and, for all we know, any day now in Estonia with respect to the use of violence against civilians and the imposition of Soviet control over the democratically elected governments of these Baltic republics.

I am asking the Secretary of State for External Affairs, not quarrelling with his analysis of the strength of the Prime Minister's statement but recognizing the urgency of the situation there that some action be taken: What can Canada do today at the United Nations to bring this issue into the international arena where it belongs?
I suggest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that he not let the Soviet veto get in the way. If the Soviets want to veto some suggestion by Canada, so be it, but Canada should be making concrete suggestions as to how this can be dealt with at the UN.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I accept that and I agree with that. There is of course an extension between making a case and having a direct effect. I accept the hon. member's case that despite the veto there may well be things we should be doing at the UN and indeed in the CSCE.
I think the most practical thing I could do today is to accept the opportunity as a parliamentarian to meet the vice-president of Latvia who is here, and I have changed my schedule to do that.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure everyone welcomes the willingness of the minister to meet with these groups, but in the end he will have to act on behalf of the government and not as a parliamentarian. What we are trying to suggest are ways and things that the government can do.
Therefore, I have a supplementary question having to do with the direct assistance option of which the minister spoke. I am in receipt of information which the government may already have of the various medical needs of the republic of Lithuania and certainly now of the republic of Latvia as a result of the actions taken by the Soviet troops.
I wonder whether the government is now making plans to deliver that kind of medical aid, equipment, et cetera, drugs and various other things that are needed in those republics as a result of Soviet action.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the short answer to that question is yes.
Indeed we have had discussions with some provincial governments which have indicated a willingness to make
Oral Questions
some contributions to medical aid. We are looking at other ways in which we can both assemble the aid and ensure that it reaches its destination. The latter problem may prove more difficult than the former, but I have some confidence that that can be accomplished. I would appreciate, naturally, the help of members of the House in identifying sources of medical aid that may be helpful to Canada and helpful to the people of the Baltic republics in this circumstance.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs and it concerns the treatment of prisoners of war.
In light of the parading of the coalition prisoners of war on Iraqi television over the weekend which gives cause for concern for their treatment, I wonder if the Secretary of State for External Affairs could tell the House what assurances Canada has sought to ensure that prisoners of war are treated by the Iraqis according to the 1949 Geneva Convention on the treatment of prisoners of war.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have today called in the ambassador of Iraq to Canada to demand precisely those undertakings. That is Iraq's clear obligation under international law, and Canada expects it to adhere absolutely to those obligations.

I thank the minister for his direct answer. I am sure he is doing all within his power to talk with Iraq.
Those of us in the House who have looked at some of the things they have done, even before the war, would have great cause and indeed wonder if they would honour these commitments.
I would ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to give us perhaps his assurance or response to the proposal that we may have to go outside the Iraqi ambassador and indeed seek assurances from international organizations directly, like, for example, the International Red Cross.

January 21, 1991
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

Mr. Speaker, I am certainly prepared to do that.
I would remind the hon. member that when there was an agreement by the world, indeed an agreement that had been initiated by Canada with regard to trying to get food and medical supplies to people in particular need in Iraq by way of the International Red Cross, it was Saddam Hussein who said no, just as he has said no throughout this piece.
It would be extremely unwise for anyone to assume that, until he is forced to, Saddam Hussein is going to change a position which has consistently, day after day, using all the time that we have given him, put the world more and more at risk.

speechtext:
