Can the Prime Minister reassure Canadian journalists that our traditional freedom of the press will co-exist with security in a war zone for the duration of this conflict?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, indeed the Canadian forces are under Canadian command. Any journalists who are there will obviously be given full freedom of the press, subject of course to all necessary requirements stipulated by military authorities in a war zone.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, but the question is: Whose authority? The Canadian Association of Journalists complains that our reporters are subject to U.S. censorship.
Can the Minister of National Defence assure this House that Canadian reporters will be able to tell the full story of our forces and the job they are doing to the Canadian people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as of last Friday, I signed a letter to the president of Canadian Press, which represents the media located in the Persian Gulf area. I outlined exactly the attitude and the opportunities available for the Canadian media to be briefed and to be brought up to date without
harming the operational capability of the Canadian forces.
I cannot guarantee for other nations or I cannot guarantee that Canadian media located in other countries where Canadian military authorities are not functioning can have the same access. I am sure people will recognize the consistency with which we have dealt with the media, and that will continue.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
One of the factors which has made the public skeptical of the war in the gulf, in particular the motives of western governments, has been the role of western governments over the past 10 years in the sale of arms to Iraq, against which this government is sending our forces. I raised this issue in the House last November. Has the government investigated the role of Canadian government departments and Canadian companies in the sale of arms to Iraq and if so, what can the government report to the House?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, we have looked at that. The hon. member will know that there were some unsubstantiated allegations by a Canadian journalist with regard to a particular transaction. We have asked for any evidence that journalist might have. He has provided us with none. All of the evidence we have indicates that his alleged facts are wrong.
The hon. member will also know that I have tightened the export control restrictions generally with respect to export of goods to that region which might be used as arms. I believe there have been no Canadian shipments. Again, if the hon. member has any hard evidence, not unsubstantiated allegations, not allegations in the air, I would like to look at them.
Finally, it is going to be very important for the world to seize the opportunity when this war is over to have a more effective regime. I have spoken about that. Among the steps that our diplomats are taking now, as we look to what Canada might do, what initiative we might take after the crisis is over, is an identification of the practical measures that might be taken to stop the trade of arms, not only into Iraq but into that volatile region.

Mr. Speaker, I have information that Iraq now has in place artillery capable of firing shells with high explosive or chemical warheads at extended ranges, shells which were tested by a private Belgian company in 1987-88 at the Department of National Defence Research Centre at Suffield, Alberta.
If the Department of National Defence did not know this, and I am advised that it could have known it by simple inquiries, that the shells were destined for Iraq, can the minister tell us whether the government was aware of this? Will the minister agree that an immediate, independent, public investigation be launched into Canadian involvement in all arms sales to Iraq?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am still not aware of anything other than the allegation which has just been made by the hon. member. If he is serious, he will provide us right now-lay it upon the table of the House, or deliver it to me directly-all of the information that he has that we should be pursuing.
On the basis of the information I have, there has been no Canadian involvement in that trade. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I am pleased that the hon. member now understands that Saddam Hussein does possess this deadly capacity and if we had given him the time, which the hon. member and his party asked us to give him, he would have made more deadly use of that potential.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It concerns the very serious human rights violations in Latvia and the other Baltic countries.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs is aware that the third round of the CSCE conference on the human dimension, the human rights conference, is being held in Moscow later this summer with the U.S.S.R as host. Surely we should be thinking about bringing some pressure to perhaps relocate that meeting to another country or withdrawing from it.
Oral Questions
I think it would be a tragedy, if the U.S.S.R. does not change their approach, for us to attend a human rights conference in Moscow.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the decision was taken to have the conference of the CSCE in Moscow, I believe Canada was the last country of the CSCE to agree to that location. We did so with some reluctance, precisely because we wanted to have some guarantees as to the commitment of the Soviet Union to human rights matters.
It was the judgment of the Government of Canada at that time that it was very important to have a conference on that topic in the atmosphere of perestroika and glasnost within the Soviet Union. We have secured guarantees with respect to access of journalists, the position of non-governmental organizations and the like.
I agree with the hon. member that the events in the Baltic republics raise questions that must be considered with regard to that meeting. I think he would agree with me that it would be well for the Government of Canada and others to respond, prudently and carefully, to that proposal, so what I will do is note a proposal that has been made by a member of the House.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Is the minister preparing to honour this agreement when the U.S. suffers a shortage as a result of what the Prime Minister has predicted to be a long and difficult war in the Persian Gulf?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, with respect to the free trade agreement, I point out to the hon. member that chapter 9, the energy chapter, commits both signatories to all the obligations that they had taken before that, principally, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
As well, I remind the hon. member that in 1974 the then Liberal government joined Canada-and I agree

Oral Questions
with that-in the International Energy Agency, whereby Canada obligated itself for sharing of any shortfalls. It is that obligations which Canada is following and not the free trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the same minister. Could he confirm that the government has prepared a gas rationing plan for consumers and that ration coupons are about to be printed, in fact, are being printed at this very moment in Cornwall?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada, along with the provinces and the industry, has developed an oil and gas industry in which our reserves have, in fact, increased since the days of the latter seventies and the early eighties.
Second, I point out to her that we are in a position where we are a net exporter of oil and gas.
Third, it is for these reasons that this government has spent a lot of money in encouraging new projects, both in the west and off the east coast, so that we can increase our supply.
Last, under the International Energy Agreement, there are three stages, one of public information, the second a co-ordinated emergency response mechanism which we triggered after the invasion and, third, if there should be rationing, as part of the IEA- which we do not believe will happen-we have not printed coupons. If we were to ever come to that point, it was the Liberal government of 1974 that committed Canada to that approach.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. On Friday, the Leader of the Opposition asked the government if it would provide humanitarian aid to the people of Israel, in light of the unprovoked attack upon it by Saddam Hussein and in light of our sympathy and solidarity with that country and the Prime Minister said that such aid had been offered. I ask the Prime Minister if he can provide the
House with the details of this humanitarian aid at this time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my colleague and I pointed out in the House, not on Friday but on Tuesday, we believed that the ultimate ambition of Saddam Hussein was to launch an attack against Israel. This is one of the reasons why Canada has taken such a firm stand in defending the United Nations and its principles because that was consistent with the avoidance of the kind of attacks we have seen against Israel.
When the attacks took place, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and I immediately conveyed to the Prime Minister of Israel and his government our expressions of solidarity and support, together with our intention to be of assistance in respect of any humanitarian requirements that might arise.
We have been keeping in touch both with the government of Israel and with leaders of the Jewish community across Canada. We have not yet received a specific demand, but the Government of Israel has expressed great appreciation for the understanding, support and solidarity manifested by the government and the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in light of all these contacts, I again ask the Prime Minister if he can tell us more about this aid which will be welcomed by all concerned, and in particular if he can tell us exactly what this aid will consist of.
When will it be sent? Will it help repair the damage caused by the missiles? Also, will it help provide housing for the hundreds of thousands of refugees crowding into Israel because of conditions in the Soviet Union?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member at the end of his question raises another matter which has to do with housing and refugees.
When I was in Israel in November, there were discussions with regard to Canadian assistance for housing. We said that we would be prepared to have Canada involved in that kind of assistance provided it did not have to do with housing in the occupied territories.
With regard to the humanitarian assistance, it would come from CIDA. Sources have been identified. The government of Israel has, very recently, not only indicated its appreciation of the help that was offered but
January 21, 1991

suggested that at this stage it was an offer which, while appreciated, would not be taken up at this stage.
We have also made a similar offer to the government of Jordan. The Jordanians also indicated that because the reports had been exaggerated of the impact of missiles falling on their territory they would not respond at this stage.
I should take the opportunity, since it relates to humanitarian assistance to Jordan, to say that I have discussed with Jordanian officials help that Canada might provide to Jordan in dealing with refugees who might come into that country as a result of their decision, taken at the urging of the world, to open their border to refugees from Iraq or elsewhere.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence.
We are hearing reports in generalization of carpet bombing of Iraq day after day and night after night, but because of military censorship we are not getting any of the facts about casualties which, judging by World War II experience, potentially can be very devastating.
Will the minister give us some estimate from his sources of how many people-men, women and children-military or civilian, have been killed in this carpet bombing?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the only estimate I can give him is that which Saddam Hussein put forward from Iraq. The fatalities are less than 100.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
King Hussein of Jordan recently called for a temporary ceasefire to give dialogue and diplomacy a chance to avert a tragic disaster. Will the Secretary of State for External Affairs comment as to what is Canada's response to King Hussein's call?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The Government of Canada
Routine Proceedings
has maintained the most active possible contact with King Hussein and with his government.
We thought that was particularly necessary because other governments involved in the coalition were not maintaining that contact. That is the reason I visited Jordan in November, and that is the reason why the Prime Minister has been in regular communication with the King. That is why I phoned Mr. Masri, the foreign minister two days ago. We are maintaining close contact with him.
Our ambassador, Percy Sherwood, was called in by King Hussein two nights ago. King Hussein expressed to him his deep appreciation of the leadership that Canada has shown in keeping lines open between members of the coalition and Jordan.
With respect to the particular proposal that King Hussein has put forward, that is one with which we disagree. We think it would be inappropriate for there to be a pause or a cease-fire until Saddam Hussein has used the channels that are open to him to indicate clearly that he is prepared to accept Security Council resolutions that were duly passed, and that he had an opportunity to accept in conditions of peace and they now are being enforced by the world.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I move, pursuant to Standing Order 52, seconded by the hon. member for LaSalle-Emard, for leave to adjourn the House for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the turmoil in the Baltic states.
Although the House of Commons recently passed a resolution on the situation, I strongly feel that events over the weekend in Latvia and the increase in military activity in all three states warrant serious discussion on the future of Canada's relations with the Soviet Union.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 BALTIC STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the motion of the House of January 15 condemning the Soviet Union on its policy in the Baltic states, I request under Standing Order 52 leave to have an emergency debate on the aggression against the Baltic nations by uncontrolled special forces of the Soviet Union.
A genuine emergency has arisen due to the fact that the duly elected governments of Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania are under siege by an aggressor. We cannot reward aggression, that precedent being established by the coalition against Iraq.
I am calling for an immediate debate, as well, because international law has been broken by a foreign power, the U.S.S.R., as Canada has never recognized the forceful annexation of those Baltic states.
As Your Honour is aware of the new developments in the Baltic states since the motion of the House on January 15, the debate being of urgency should take priority over the day-to-day business of the House.

subtopic: EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in third reading of this bill. We can view with some gratification, indeed some anticipation, the likely outcome of the initiative which is embodied in this piece of legislation.
No one in this House or indeed anyone in the western world can do other than welcome the extraordinary events in eastern Europe over the past year or 18 months which have led to the proposal now before us to create a European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. It is not very many years ago when the concept of a bank embracing both the countries of eastern and western Europe, and indeed countries outside Europe, in a common effort to bring about the more rapid economic development of the now united continent of Europe would have been virtually unthinkable.
Yet here we are today with a bill before the House for third reading which will bring about Canada's participation in the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. It will enable Canada to contribute to the resources of the bank and make Canada one of its founding members.
We on this side of the House welcome the development of the idea first broached by President Mitterrand in the summer of 1989. We welcome Canada's participation and we look forward to the early date when the bank will play a major role in giving further substance to the unification that we have seen in Europe.
This is primarily a bank with the purpose of channelling funds into the now market-oriented economies of central and eastern Europe. It is a bank which will be committed to providing funds for those nations in central and eastern Europe which demonstrate the principles of multi-party democracy, of pluralism, and market economics.
Canada's participation in the bank will be substantial. We shall hold 3.4 per cent of the shares in the bank. We shall over a period of five years contribute some $150 million toward the capital of the bank. That is a contribution and a participation that ranks Canada among the more active members of the bank.
In passing I would ask of the government whether in terms of participation in the bank what has become of the fact that the original terms under which the bank was proposed envisaged a role for the German Democratic
Government Orders
Republic. Should we now assume that those shares will be picked up by the Federal Republic of Germany, the now united Germany, and, if so, will that make Germany the largest single participant in the bank?
If one assumes that the German Democratic Republic and the Federal Republic shares are to be merged into the shares of the now united Germany, it would indeed make Germany the largest participant in the bank, with a few shares more than that of the United States, which in the original planning was to have been the largest single participant.
I would ask the government, before we finish our brief discussion of this bill, whether it might respond to that particular question.
As I have noted, the legislation before us makes it clear, as does the bank's articles of constitution, that the principal purpose of the new bank will be to channel funds to private enterprise, the market-oriented economies of central and eastern Europe. Throughout eastern Europe, there is a great need to promote private and individual initiatives.
All of us, I am sure, on every side of this House, look toward such an initiative as a major way of underpinning the developments of the last 18 months in eastern Europe. It can help to give substance to the desire on the part of the eastern European countries to move away from the communist regimes which have marked their post-war history to the open market economies that have contributed so substantially to the contrasting prosperity in western Europe.
In addition, we on this side of the House, and I am sure all members, welcome the fact that some major part of the funds of the bank will be directed toward the necessary restructuring of the public goods and services of eastern Europe. I speak principally of questions pertaining to the environment which have been sadly neglected in eastern Europe in the post-war years. In addition, funds will be directed to the public works which are in most eastern European countries in need of refurbishment or of replacement.
We shall see, I think, a major demand on the bank's resources in the time ahead will be to contribute to the environmental clean-up, the infrastructure and perhaps, most important, the reform of state-owned corporations. But the principal purpose, and I think we should not lose sight of that, is that the bank will promote the development of market-oriented economies through eastern Europe, a type of economy to which the countries of

January 21, 1991
Government Orders
eastern Europe have clearly and consistently in the past months committed themselves.
In conclusion, one comment that has been raised in regard to the creation of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, which is to be situated in London, is that somehow it conflicts with the machinery and the potential of the World Bank, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, to channel funds to eastern Europe. For my part, I would not accept that the existence of the IBRD is a valid argument against the creation of the European Bank. Of course, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Monetary Fund will have a continuing role to play in the growth and renewal of the economies of eastern Europe. The fact remains, however, that within the United Nations system, the regional banks have been recognized as playing a substantial role in providing capital for the particular needs of the major regions of the world. Obviously, the Asian Development Bank has had considerable success in channelling funds into development projects in Asia, as has the Inter-American Development Bank in Latin America and the African Development Bank in that continent.
It is both consistent and natural that in the particular circumstances facing the countries of eastern Europe today, a special regional bank for Europe should also be created. Such a bank will be the best place to identify and to develop the projects that this common effort on the part of countries, not only in Europe but outside Europe, can hope to offer. It is for that reason and indeed for a variety of other reasons that we welcome this legislation pledging Canadian participation in the creation of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

Mr. Speaker, I will begin my comments on this bill by saying that there is a certain irony in the fact that we are debating this bill today at the same time that we are contemplating an emergency debate this evening on the situation in the Baltic republics.
One of the things that people have been discussing is what actions might be taken with respect to our relationship with the Soviet Union because of events in the Baltic.
Yet, here we are this afternoon sort of uncritically debating the establishment of a bank. I am not saying this in a critical way. I am just pointing out the irony of it. This bank is designed to relate not only to the countries of eastern and central Europe but also the Soviet Union.
Certainly this is part of the new relationship with the Soviet Union that has come about as a result of glasnost and perestroika. If in fact those movements within the Soviet Union are now being called into question as a result of the violence against civilians in Lithuania and just the other day in Riga, Latvia, then it is difficult to talk about this new bank being set up to further that new relationship, when we are in some doubt about the
January 21, 1991

nature of that relationship as a result of the events in the Baltic.
Having said that, I think it is probably useful to go on because there is a deadline, as I understand it, to meet for the international agreement that would set up this bank, although that deadline is March 31, 1991. We are talking about some time.
I want to make it clear that I am not suggesting that we make any premature judgment about whether or not this bank is still a good idea. I think it is a good idea, but the fact that the Soviet Union is included in its ambit is perhaps something that is at least ironic, given events in the last few weeks in the Baltics.
We are all concerned about what is happening there. I had the occasion on Friday to visit with the Soviet ambassador to Canada, along with the hon. member for Scarborough and the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park, to express on behalf of the Canadian parliamentary group for the Baltic peoples our concern at what was happening in the Baltic states.
I may have more to say about that later this evening, if we get an emergency debate. Just in case, I wanted to say that that had happened and to say that we do not accept the official Soviet position put forward by the ambassador that all that is needed to solve the situation in the Baltic republics is for the Baltic republics to follow the newly established constitutional procedures for separation.
As you may know, Mr. Speaker, these procedures call for a five-year procedure by which republics would separate themselves from the Soviet Union. This is often cited by official Soviet spokespersons as the procedure which the Baltic republics should follow.
It goes unsaid in this kind of analysis, first of all, that the governments of the Baltic republics do not want to separate by virtue of a constitutional process because they continue to maintain they were illegally annexed into the Soviet Union. Therefore, for them to seek sovereignty through the established constitutional process of the Soviet Union would be for them to admit in a way they are unprepared to admit that they are in fact a part of the Soviet Union.
They wish to have a special negotiation with the Soviet Union, which recognizes the fact that a great part of the world, including themselves, never recognized their annexation by the Soviet Union. This is a position
Government Orders
supported by the Canadian government and by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade which had opportunity to go to the Soviet Union in April to meet with a variety of people, including representatives from Lithuania, about the Baltic situation.
The committee recommended that the special case of the Baltics be recognized, as it already has been by the Canadian government, by the Soviet Union. The committee recommended that the Soviet Union recognize the special status of the Baltic republics and hoped that the Soviet government and President Gorbachev might see their way through to being able to accept this special status of the Baltics and at the same time recognize that this did not necessarily set precedents for other republics which came into the Soviet Union in a different way. It was not as a result of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact of 1938.
There were plenty of grounds within the thinking of the international community for the Soviet Union to seize upon the special status of the Baltics and to have entered into meaningful negotiation with the newly elected governments of the Baltic republics, all of which were elected in 1990 as a result of the first real elections in those republics since before 1940.
I had the privilege of being there for one of those elections, the election in Lithuania in February 1990, with other members of this House, and saw first hand the authenticity and the civility with which the election in Lithuania was held. It strikes me as even more tragic the violence which is being visited upon the people of Lithuania and Latvia knowing, as I do, first hand the tremendous spirit of peaceful change through which these events happened and continue to happen in Lithuania.
All that is required, it seems to me, is for the leadership in the Soviet Union to determine first of all that the democratically elected governments of these republics not be overthrown by violence, not be overthrown at all but particularly not be overthrown by violence in the way some people have suggested is imminent. If Moscow, President Gorbachev or whoever the powers that be are now in Moscow were to allow that to happen, this would certainly mean a fundamental change in our attitude toward what is going on in the Soviet Union.

Government Orders
Let those governments continue to exist. Call back the black berets and others who are involved in these military actions against police loyal to their democratically elected governments and negotiate. It is okay for Moscow to negotiate toughly. It is okay for it to take a hard line with respect to what sovereignty might mean. It is okay for it to have its own position. I think it has a lot of legitimate concerns with respect to Baltic sovereignty, from security concerns to various economic concerns, to concerns about minorities within the Baltic republics and how they might be treated by the ethnic majorities in those Baltic republics.
There are plenty of things to be worked out and worked out over a long period of time in all likelihood, but worked out; not resolved by the swinging barrel of a Soviet tank, by automatic gunfire or by the ways in which we have seen the problem approached in the last few weeks in Lithuania and in Latvia.
In this respect I want to say that I think the rebuilding of eastern and central Europe often characterized, particularly with the coming down of the Berlin wall, the end of the Second World War, the last legacy of the Second World War. We need to realize that until the status of the Baltic republics is dealt with, the Second World War really has not come to an end in the way in which many now speak of the situation in Europe.
The Berlin wall was not the last legacy of the Second World War. The fact that the Baltic states are a part of the Soviet Union and not able to assert their independence is the last legacy of the Second World War. Until that issue is wrapped up in the appropriate way, perhaps we should refrain from suggesting that all the consequences of the Second World War have come to an end. Certainly they are where they are as a result of an agreement between Adolf Hitler and Joseph Stalin. I do not think that can be separated from the history of the Second World War. That is why I say we should perhaps refrain from language which suggests that all the consequences of the Second World War have now been dealt with. They have not been.
One thing that needs to be dealt with, as a result of the democratically expressed will of all the countries of eastern and central Europe to be integrated into the
global economy in a way in which they were not previously integrated, is how that is done. This bank is one of the measures contemplated, recommended, and is now in the process of being formed to help eastern and central Europe become integrated into that world economy.
I have a lot of problems with the economy into which they are being integrated. They will find that the streets will not be paved with gold as they enter into this new globalized capitalist economy. They will be entering that globalized capitalist economy at the worst possible time. Even if they had chosen to enter-and I am sure they would have done it in a more step-by-step way-or tried to integrate themselves more into the global economy back in 1968 when Alexander Dubcek first contemplated changing the nature of communism in Czechoslovakia, they would have had an easier time. At that time the kinds of mixed economies which might have made a transition period less difficult were more tolerated by the global economy.
Now it seems to me that these eastern and central European economies will have to go full circle and become full market capitalist economies, cold turkey so to speak, without any of the instruments at their disposal by which many western economies over the years shielded themselves, and appropriately so, from some of the tougher realities that enter in when one gets into a kind of truly global dog-eat-dog economy.
I am very pessimistic about what some of the consequences might be if this transition turns out to be too difficult. If people find, in the absence of the old system, that the new system is not yet able to deliver certain basic realities and needs like food, we may yet see a considerable political instability and unrest in those countries.
It behoves the west to put its money where its mouth has been for 45 years. We ought not to find ourselves in the position where it might be said of us that we shed all these crocodile tears for 45 years about the poor suffering people of eastern and central Europe, and for that matter the Soviet Union, because they were suffering under this particular system and yet, when they finally take the decision to break out of that system and say to us that they need our assistance in doing so to ensure that the transition is a transition which preserves democracy and which does not lead to political unrest and
January 21, 1991

instability, we simply say: "Well, we have problems of our own now and you look after yourself".
If we have learned anything from recent events, it is that there is no such thing as an isolated event. If the reforms in the Soviet Union, in particular but also eastern and central Europe, were to come crashing down as a result of economic failure, it would have repercussions for everyone concerned.
It is not just a matter of saying, "Well, you know, it is a tough world out there. It is a global marketplace. Welcome to the global marketplace. The race goes to the swiftest and the strongest. If you are not able to cut the mustard, well, too bad". I am sorry. It is not going to work like that.
If certain countries are not able to integrate themselves into the globalized economy in a way that is acceptable to their populations, then we will continue to have very serious problems in Europe, not the least of which, Mr. Speaker, might be the reality of millions of economic refugees, tens of millions of people simply packing their bags and moving west.
Many people are concerned about this in Germany, France and other parts of Europe, that if the new expectations in eastern and central Europe are not met, the so-called western Europe will be faced with a flood of refugees. So there is no small measure of self-interest in making sure that the economic expectations raised by the dismantling of the command economies in formerly communist countries succeed, that those expectations are met.
In the long term, Mr. Speaker, we look forward to the day when these countries of eastern and central Europe will be fully integrated into the European community. I think that is the long-term expectation of those countries. Many of those countries, and certainly member countries now in the European Community someday will be looking at a fully integrated Europe, in which sovereignty, particularly economic sovereignty, will be ceded at a certain level to a supranational body, in this case, the European Community headquartered in Brussels.
Hopefully, within that larger supranational framework, we might see a time when a lot of the national, ethnic and regional rivalries might find ways of expressing themselves, not in outmoded 19th century nationalist feelings, but in appropriate regional and ethnic autono-
Govemment Orders
mies that find their place within this larger supranational reality.
The sovereignty of the nation state is eroded in two ways, downwards in a devolving sort of way towards forms of regional and ethnic autonomy, that might, for instance, meet the needs of the Croats in Yugoslavia or for that matter the Scots in Great Britain, and eroding upwards towards a larger regional reality in which economic sovereignty has been ceded to that greater authority.
What is also happening in Europe, and what I think is hopeful, is people are realizing that if there is to be that kind of integrated market economy, there also needs to be a basic agreement about social standards, income security, pensions, welfare policy and various other things.
If you are going to have this kind of competitive level playing field integrated economy on a regional basis, you also have to have agreements about what the floor is in terms of social justice so that one country is not able to play its workers off against workers in another country. That has implications for analysis of the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States, all of which I do not have time to go into because I understand that my time is running out, but I hope that my comments have been helpful.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just a few words concerning this bill before the House. The bill really puts $120 million-that is not Canadian dollars, but American dollars-forward by Canada. When we go to the schedule of the bill, we find that the agreement establishing the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, states:
Considering the importance of close and co-ordinated cooperation in order to promote the economic progress of Central and Eastern European countries to help their economies become more internationally competitive and assist them in their reconstruction and development and thus to reduce, where appropriate, any risks related to the financing of their economies";
When I read those words I immediately thought about the fact that the German Democratic Republic, Poland, Bulgaria, U.S.S.R. are more competitive, more able to compete with eastern Canada for our great fishing resource than we are.
Let me mention some of the the allocations given by the Government of Canada for this year, 1991. The allocation for Bulgaria is 750 tonnes of redfish. Next to

Government Orders
them is Cuba, but it has allocations everywhere. Then there is the German Democratic Republic, which really does not exist because everybody knows what happened to the German Democratic Republic. However, it is part of the EEC. It has a quota for 1991 in zone 3L and 3N on Canada's coast of 476 metric tons of redfish. The Government of Canada has not said it yet but I suppose the allocation to the German Democratic Republic for 1991 will be folded into the EEC because there is no other way to have it. The German Democratic Republic does not exist except under the EEC as it relates to these agreements which have been signed with the Government of Canada.
Then there is Poland. They have a new allocation for this coming year of 500 metric tons of cod in zone 3M off the east coast of Canada. That zone is known internationally as the Flemish Cap, a massive spawning area for fish off the east coast of Canada. It is a shallow area in the Atlantic Ocean about 230 nautical miles east northeast of St. John's, Newfoundland.
Traditionally there has never been any fishing there. In other words, all the countries of the world got together with their scientists and they said that the entire world should respect that area and not fish it because because it is a spawning ground for a great many of our flatfish in the world, but it is also a nursery area for some of our midwater fish.
We agreed no more fishing. But this year that area has been reopened and Poland has an allocation of 500 metric tons, and Canada has an allocation of 100 metric tonnes.
We come then to the U.S.S.R. They have an allocation of 1,270 tonnes. Canada has an allocation of 100 tonnes. That is only a tiny bit of the story. Mr. Speaker, if you want to know the entire story, you would be shocked because this is only one way that eastern European countries get quotas of fish along our coastline in Canada.
As I have just noted, one of the new zones opened now sees Canada with even less allocation than the eastern European countries. One way they get quotas is through what we call NAFO, the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization. There is a similar organization off Europe.
However, we have an organization here that allows foreign nations to fish inside our zone. That is one way. The second way they get allocations is when Canada says that it is going to give out part of its own allocation.
What did we have in the month of December, around Christmas? We had Poland with special licences for mackerel in 4VWX. That is along the east coast of Nova Scotia, in 4VN, which is up around Cape Breton Island, and 5ZE, which is down further off New Brunswick.
Bulgaria has mackerel and silver hake licences in 4VN. The Soviet Union had at least 40 factory ships that had licences at that time. It must be kept in mind that these vessels are there because they can compete with Canadian vessels. The reason for it is quite simple.
Today in Canada we have five large companies that actually hire vessels from eastern Europe to catch their own quotas along the coastline of Canada.
Fisheries Products International is the biggest fish company we have. On January 4, U.S.S.R. vessels were unloading turbot at their fish plants to keep their fish plants going. Imagine, the Soviet Union unloading fish at FPI. It is a new phenomenon in Canada, and it just came about this past year. Never before have we ever had foreign nations whose vessels were used to catch fish in Canadian waters on licences owned by Canadian companies.
The question asked is: why? Canadian fishermen are the best fishermen in the world. They are more competitive, one would say, than any other fishermen in the world. They know how to catch fish better than any other fishermen in the world. They are the best in the world.
Why is it that for the past year or so these Canadian companies have received permission from the Government of Canada to employ vessels from eastern Europe, from the very countries we are talking about here today under this bill that will establish a bank that will see Canadian input to help these eastern European countries? The answer is quite simple.
A lot of these companies from eastern Europe and the governments from eastern Europe do not really mind if they lose money. They do not mind if they are out for 10 months fishing on the Atlantic Ocean or the Pacific Ocean, and they do not catch anything. So, they are more competitive than a Canadian vessel would be.

My intervention in this debate today is to make a simple suggestion to the Government of Canada. That is, if we are truly going to follow through on the intent of this legislation, it should not be a question of subsidizing a company or a country to be more competitive. It should be a question of making everything a level playing field.
The first thing the Government of Canada should do is to cancel every licence in Canadian waters held by foreign nations for fish which are under quotas to Canadian fishermen. That is the first thing the Government of Canada should do. That is my suggestion to the Government of Canada in passing this legislation.
We are the ones who are not competitive in the fishing industry, simply because we do not have the financial muscle that some of these governments put into their fishing vessels. I suggest to the Government of Canada, cancel the licences and give Canadians a chance in the fishing industry in eastern Canada.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I certainly do. First, we could assist many of these countries in showing them that certain types of machinery used on a massive scale can destroy an environment. In other words, the term "sustainable development", that the Liberal Party of Canada uses quite a bit in formulating policy, should be the first and foremost thing that we should promote with these nations.

It is unbelievable to imagine that you could be sitting in a control room on a vessel and, through computers, be able to control the nets and so on that go over the bottom of the ocean. That is what happens in many of these vessels.
Government Orders
Also, this gear makes no distinction between the age of fish, none at all. It does not make any distinction between dragging over a nursery ground or a spawning ground, or dragging up the food of the very fish of which we have so few in our country.
We could give these countries the scientific knowledge that we have in Canada today and institute the same measures that we have in Canada for our resources. That is, we have a policy in Canada that says the Speaker of the House of Commons is not allowed to go commercial fishing in Canada. A member of Parliament is not allowed to go fishing if he wants. An unemployed man down the road is not allowed to go fishing, because we have completely controlled entry in the fishery. We have strict management, heavy fines, and good environmental protection that these countries do not have. That is one contribution we can make.
Another contribution we can make is to suggest to some of these nations other ways of obtaining fish. I refer, of course, to the economy of growing fish. That is one area in which we could make a great contribution to the eastern European countries, the area of growing fish, but certainly not in the area of using massive large vessels to travel all the way across the Atlantic Ocean to catch fish that nobody over here is allowed to catch and, in the bargain, to destroy some of our resources, as resources have been destroyed right around the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know the hon members on the government side are calling for the question, but I believe the bill is too important to let it go by without some further debate.
It was not long ago that the countries named in Annex A of this bill rejoiced because President Gorbachev brought in glasnost and perestroika. How the world rejoiced when finally a leader of the Soviet Union took off the shackles and yokes from the people and said: "Fine, tell us what you want. Tell us what kind of governments you want and what kind of commerce you want." The world cheered President Gorbachev. It even presented him with a Nobel Peace Price.
Thanks to the leadership of President Gorbachev and the western world, the cold war finally came to an end. I was with the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade in East Berlin on May 1 when thousands upon thousands of people crossed from East Berlin to West Berlin and back without even having to show a passport or a visa.

Government Orders
Twenty years ago, I lived in an east European country for a full year. One does not get to know a country by going through the country as a tourist, but I lived in Poland for a full year. From Poland I travelled to Czechoslovakia, Hungary, and all of the countries listed in Annex A-Romania, Yugoslavia and Bulgaria. The only countries we could not visit at that time were the Soviet Union and Albania. I mention this because I think it highlights how far we have come from 1970-71 to 1990-91. Now we are free to travel through most of the Soviet Union republics and even through Albania.
Many of these countries that I have mentioned have had free elections. We remember how many lives were lost in achieving free democratic parliaments.
Some people forget when the Solidarity movement really started. When I lived in Poland in 1970-71, there were the first food riots where 56 people were killed. From that to today, we have come a long, long way.
These countries have now shed communism and elected democratic forms of government. I was in Lithuania when it had its free elections on February 24.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that Lithuania, followed by Latvia and Estonia, did follow the secret ballot elections. Anyone who wanted to represent a party or run as an independent could run. Their names were on the ballot and people voted. Through secret ballot votes, we now have all these democratic parliaments.
But what has the West done to help these countries with their economic and political reforms? Yes, we have all sorts of programs. For example, the government has assigned $72 million to help Hungary and Poland. We have seen good evidence of farmers coming from there to learn our expertise and techniques in farming. We have had programs in management. We have had programs in teaching English to many of the people in eastern Europe. But I do not think the West has
seriously addressed the problems of how these countries can move to a private enterprise economy.
Under Bill C-88, this bank for the restructuring and the development of the central eastern Europe economies is one major way of showing the world that the West is ready to come to their aid.
I have heard even today that maybe we should reconsider passing Bill C-88. When it was at first and second reading, there was no cold war. There was excellent co-operation between the Soviet Union and Canada. That co-operation, sadly, ended a little over a week ago when the Red Army moved in to Vilnius. I was there. I recognized the streets and the buildings that are being attacked by the Black Berets and the tanks, overnight destroying what has taken so long to build.
This weekend, we saw five more innocent people, civilians and journalists, killed. Why? For what reason? The hon. member for Scarborough Centre and I met with about 500 people just this Saturday. There were Canadian representatives from the three Baltic groups and representatives from the countries. There were young people from Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. They gave us firsthand accounts of what is happening there. I will save that for the emergency debate that I hope we will have later this day in the House.
I do not share the view that we should not pass this bill. Let us hope that President Gorbachev will get some sense into his head and remove any trace of Soviet armies in the Baltic states so that we can get back to the kind of dialogue we have had.
Was it not nice when President Gorbachev could visit Canada, when our Prime Minister could visit the Soviet Union, and when we could sign all sorts of agreements and co-operate? How beautiful. The world rejoiced. Now, in just two weekends, we have ruined all of this.
I hope that the leaders and the people of the world know that we are all one family on this planet and that somehow we will resolve our differences, work together, and, maybe through a structure such as the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, we can provide much stronger help to eastern European countries who want to get on their feet again.
There are four million Canadians who are directly tied with central and eastern Europe, so we have a vested interest in helping these countries. I want to thank the
January 21, 1991

government for accepting our amendment stressing the environmental issues, that when the bank does give a loan the first thing it will look at is this project in keeping with sustainable development. All three parties agreed to that and it is now in the bill, strengthening the bill, again demonstrating to the public how if we all work together we come up with something better. With the three parties working here together, we have come up with a better bill.
We on this side will not stall. We just want to put our comments on the record and support this bill wholeheartedly with a caution to President Gorbachev if he wants this bill to work because the Soviet Union is a donor and can be as well a recipient of this bank. It will be up to him whether he really and truly believes in democracy or going back to Stalinistic types of rule.

subtopic: EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT ACT
speechtext:
First of all, I want to say that we as a party support the government's proposal to establish a bank for the reconstruction of Europe, of central and eastern Europe.

Let us dwell on the background that has given rise to this development. We have seen extraordinary things coming out of Europe, largely at the instigation of a new policy and a new direction from the U.S.S.R. Perestroika and glasnost have led to the breaking up of the Iron Curtain. The Soviet Union has given up its hegemony over its Iron Curtain countries.
We have seen something which I never expected would take place in my lifetime. It was East Germany being given its freedom. Within a very short time the Berlin wall came crumbling down, and Germany has now been unified. These political events, I am sure, surpassed the greatest expectations that we could have had about the liberalization of policies in eastern Europe.
We are now asked in terms of this bill, Bill C-88, to establish the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. We see a bill whereby the European community has come to us, the western European community is going to the world and saying: "Do we not have an obligation to help the eastern European and central European countries make the transition from controlled economics and centrally-planned economies to market economies so that they can take their place in the new global community?"
I can unhesitatingly say yes, we do have that obligation.
For years after the Second World War, we have seen how the reconstruction took place. Bretton Woods was an example of how the world community came together and established the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Monetary Fund.
But that was not enough, because a devastated Europe was regarded by the Americans as a drawback to the
flourishing of the economies of all of us. It was under the generous Marshall plan and the even more generous act of the United States in establishing funding for our allies in Europe to re-establish themselves that we were able to see them start to prosper and as a result we, in North America and other parts of the world, benefited too from the expanding trade and prosperity that was won.
That was really the start of the global economic village where we realized that there is no country that can be continually prosperous unless the world is prosperous as a whole.
But we have failed miserably following the Second World War in terms of bringing along the countries of the south, the Third World countries. We did not have plans addressed to assist them in the same way we dealt with our former allies. As a result, many Third World countries, countries of the south, have gone backward in terms of their per capita income and their standards of living.
We are seeing now a devastation in terms of drought, hunger, famine and death. In the Sudan alone, up to eight million people in the south are now facing the threat of starvation. When our collective efforts have been directed, they have worked. The shame is that we have not taken these collective efforts to all people on our continually diminishing globe.
Let us return now to the situation in central Europe. As my colleague from Parkdale-High Park and as many other speakers have pointed out, we do have an obligation to work with these new economies to help them become viable. It is in their interest and it is in our long-term interest not only in terms of the politics of the moment, but in terms of building strong economies so that we all will prosper, as the Marshall plan indicated we would, by helping out our former allies.
Through Mr. Gorbachev's enlightened policies, he has made their emergence as countries possible. He does not have the economic means to ensure their prosperity. As a matter of fact, we are now seeing a falling back in the Soviet Union itself of Mr. Gorbachev's progressive policies as hardliners say to him: "Perestroika is not working. We must return to the old ways."
This is the dilemma we face, because the western world wants to see the Soviet Union and its former Iron Curtain allies turn the corner economically. We are faced with a problem, and I faced this problem-the
January 21, 1991

world did-a couple of years ago with the People's Republic of China. We wanted to see the one billion people in the PRC come out of the dark ages and develop their economy in such a way that it would be constructive, and its people could prosper and enjoy better standards of living.
Then, we were faced with the terrible political realities of Tiananmen Square which have set back western efforts to invest, to deal with and to support a regime which is so repressive.
What we have seen as well in the Baltic states gives us great cause for concern. The repression of the free expression of the people in the Baltic states of their political rights of self-expression and self-determination has been met by armed aggression. This gladdens the hearts of none of us because we had hoped that perestroika would be an ongoing process in which we could participate through an institution such as the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
Now we find ourselves tom. We have to send a message to the Soviet Union that its actions are not acceptable to Canada, that human rights must prevail, that force is not the way to deal with the free expression of ideals by the people in the Baltic states. How do we send that message to the Soviet Union and at the same time vote for Bill C-88, which does have as part of its objects aid to and the participation of the U.S.S.R.?
That is the dilemma we face on all sides of the House. This is not a political issue. My feeling is that it would be retrogressive at this time to say we will not support the construction of this bank because, after all, it is to aid many countries: Poland, Yugoslavia, Hungary, and Bulgaria. East Germany, which is now part of Germany, will probably be looked after on a bilateral basis now by Germany itself. We have an obligation to help these countries to develop their own self-sufficiency in their new market economies.
I believe in good conscience we can do so. We can pass this bill. Let us at the same time send a veiy strong message to the leadership of the U.S.S.R. that its actions in the Baltic states are not condoned. If we were not to support this bill just because of the actions of one of the members of this bank, I believe we would be setting back
Government Orders
the cause of progress in many other countries which are so important to us.
While it is with a heavy heart we recognize that perestroika is not working in the way we had hoped, let us support this bill because it is the way of the future. Let us learn from Bill C-88, the bill to establish the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, that our efforts do not lie with central and eastern Europe alone.
Let us take from this further effort and incentive to enhance the efforts of other development banks: the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Bank, and the institutions in Latin America. Let us ensure that we play our full role in the industrialization and development of the countries of this world where we must be ashamed of the level of life we accept as being normal for them.
Let us use this as an example to re-examine the fundamental hypocrisy of each of us as parliamentarians on all sides of this House and, yes, of all Canadians when we say that life is sacred, that we are aroused beyond all belief when we see people being killed by armed aggression-and we should be-but the number of people who die in this world daily from starvation, malnutrition, lack of medicine and lack of the very basics of life is far greater than those who die in a year through armed aggression.
Let us, in supporting this bill, recommit our faith to the collective obligation of all of us who are privileged to help those who are not. We are not only helping them. We are helping to build a better world order which will help us. Let us recommit our dedication to helping all people in this world.

subtopic: EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question from my hon. colleague from Parkdale-High Park.
This bank is being capitalized with $12 billion. Some 51 per cent of the contribution and the control is going to the European Community itself. This was the creation of the government of Francois Mitterrand. Then the European Community put it on its agenda at Brussels a year ago last December. Canada's contribution could be up to a total of $460 million. I do not think we will ever be called upon to put in that amount of money, as our initial commitment is $5 million.
The bank is going to use its equity base, contributed by all of its member countries, to go out and borrow on the market. It is going to try to enhance free enterprise in central and eastern Europe by making loans available to private enterprise. Its primary objective is to devote 60 per cent of its funds, the equity that is contributed, and, on top of that, the funds it is able to borrow in world financial markets to promote industries that have a chance of making it.
We have seen a vast enhancement of the ability of these formerly communistic centrally controlled economies to absorb foreign investments. In 1988 there were only 165 industrial joint ventures in these countries. Within one year, under glasnost and perestroika, the interest in investing had increased so that there were 2,100 joint ventures.
I think a joint venture is an ideal way to go into a newly emerging economy where they do not have the history of a free market and private enterprise which may exist in other areas, but where they do have a strong record of state control and co-ordination. Then there is the transition of the state working with private entrepreneurs, to bring to change what has always been 100 per cent state control toward what in other parts of the world has been 100 per cent free enterprise. One can bring together the best ingredients of both to create the transition and to make these enterprises work. This is why I feel, in terms of the 60 per cent that is to go to
investments in the private sector, we have a good chance of using joint ventures to help make the transition.
It is expected as well, in response to my hon. friend from Parkdale-High Park, that 40 per cent of these funds will have to go to build up state infrastructure. After all, we cannot have viable enterprises and industries in the global economic community unless we have an infrastructure: communications, transportation, et cetera. We have to build up the institutions that service industries, financial institutions as well.
I believe they have set what is probably a realistic target in terms of what we will have to invest in the basic infrastructure of these countries in order to produce the economic viability necessary to develop in these new economies.
As I see these investments going ahead, I see Canadians with their expertise in construction, communications, and transportation playing a major role in going in there, in investing, in providing expertise, and in creating jobs in Canada to build the necessary products to help them develop.
This is not just a giveaway. This is an investment in other countries, but this is also an investment in Canadian entrepreneurs. Over the long term it is truly an investment in a more prosperous global economy from which we will all be the ultimate beneficiaries.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that I have listened with interest to the comments of my hon. colleague from Willowdale and others, including the hon. member from Winnipeg Transcona. I must say the tone of the debate, the points being raised, indicates a considerable amount of enlightenment on behalf of members of all caucuses in terms of the potential role Canada can play. I want to congratulate my hon. friend on a number of proposals and suggestions he has just made. I must say, if I heard correctly, I pretty well agree with everything he said. I would like to take it a little further than that, but again my compliments go out to all previous speakers.
We first heard of this proposal back in 1989 by Francois Mitterrand, the President of France. He said, at a session of the European Parliament, that something had to be done in terms of industrial nations to assist countries which were being dramatically changed in central and
eastern Europe as a result of perestroika in the Soviet Union and the spin-off into the eastern European countries.
I can remember-and I remember you too, Mr. Speaker, sharing that delight-the coming down of the Berlin wall, the announcements flowing daily from President Gorbachev in terms of his view of the changing world, the move to democratization, the movement from some state enterprises toward a free market system, the recognition of the value of a mixed economy, and that the reception that received in the western world, particularly in western industrialized nations, was most positive.
Immediately we thought: How can we help? I remember thoughtful discussions with my colleagues as to ways and means that Canada could participate in assisting the countries of central Europe as they changed their economies and moved through this very difficult transition period, not only economically but, as someone like yourself would appreciate, Mr. Speaker, the social, cultural, and political implications of these dramatic changes. We are pleased.
We are not so pleased with the lack of progress in terms of economic reforms, particularly in the Soviet Union. But recognizing that there are conservative forces in the system there rallying against these dramatic changes and trying to cling to the old ways, the status quo in the Soviet Union, we abhor that position and look for more liberal approaches in terms of liberalizing the economy and the life of the average Soviet citizen. This whole debate on Bill C-88 is put in a peculiar context with the developments in the last number of hours in the Baltic states. We have witnessed the oppressive initiatives taken by Soviet troops, both in Lithuania and Latvia and recognize the growing democracy and the call for self-determination of the Baltic states. It was with heavy hearts that we watched on television the activities of the Soviet troops against the citizens of those two Baltic states.
I must say that it brings up this question: are we enthusiastic now about using Canadian taxpayers' dollars as a result of our participation in this European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, knowing that these funds will go to the Soviet Union at the same time when this abuse of human rights is occurring, not only in these two states, but elsewhere. But I am referring particularly to the coverage that we have received in the last number
Government Orders
of hours of very sad activities going on in the Baltic states.
I suppose they pale in comparison to the brutality and the unbelievable horrors of war that are unfolding in the Persian Gulf, but I will let that stand aside for now. It will be an ongoing debate, of course, the next little while. We all hope and pray that that horror show will be short and peace will come soon.
The bank, as I indicated, comes from the initiative proposed by the French President, Frangois Mitterrand, during the 1989 November session of the European Parliament. Its headquarters will be located in London, and the first president of the bank will be Jacques Attali from France. This agreement that we are discussing today from a Canadian perspective will be ratified by the end of this fiscal year, meaning March 31. We should also recognize that Canada is, I would not say a relatively small player, as we will be contributing $479 million of the bank's capital-which of course, Mr. Speaker as you know, will ensure us a seat on the board of directors, which is appropriate-in a total bank fund of $15 billion Canadian. That will come to, as the statistics indicate, something like 3.4 per cent of the bank's capital.
Again, Canada will not be a major player but an important player. Speaking on behalf of the New Democratic Party, we feel that, yes, we ought to be involved; yes, Canada has much to offer. That is not to say we do not have some concerns.
We registered our concerns in committee, particularly about Article 11 which sets out the methods of operation. I think because of this important aspect I want to read a few of the points from the legislation into the record. Before I do that, let me indicate my concern that this tremendous shift from an economy based on Stalinist bureaucracies into something that more closely resembles the reality found in other social democratic countries, other socialist countries, other capitalist countries, is something that I think we all support enthusiastically. We recognize that the transition is long overdue and we want to be behind it. However, let us not get caught up so enthusiastically that we end up hindering the transition towards a mixed economy in the eastern European countries and in the Soviet Union.
When we look at the methods of operation we wonder if in fact we are not tying one arm behind the back, so to speak, of these countries as they move through this difficult economic and social transition period. I have noticed with considerable interest the various reports

January 21, 1991
Government Orders
coming out of some of the descriptions of the IMF and World Bank funding of certain projects throughout the world and how that may in fact be almost ideologically restrictive and putting ideological blinders in terms of how those funds may be invested. I certainly do not want to see us being part of that restricting of funding. I want to read a couple of points. Article 11, under Methods of Operation, of Bill C-88 reads:
That the Bank shall carry out its operations in furtherance of its purpose and functions as set out in Articles 1 and 2 of this Agreement in any or all of the following ways:
I am sure I do not have to go through Articles 1 and 2; all of us are more than familiar with those aspects of the legislation. Article 11 goes on to state:
(i) by making, or cofinancing together with multilateral institutions, commercial banks or other interested sources, or participating in, loans to private sector enterprises, loans to any state-owned enterprise operating competitively and moving to participation in the market-oriented economy, and loans to any state-owned enterprise to facilitate its transition to private ownership and control; in particular to facilitate or enhance the participation of private and/or foreign capital in such enterprises;
It is perfectly clear, in terms of what we are asking of this legislation. I look with interest at my hon. friend, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, who is nodding that if there is one thing that is clear, it is obviously this particular paragraph.
However, I have a concern, Mr. Speaker. When the bill indicates that by making, or cofinancing together with multilateral institutions, commercial banks or other interested sources, or participating in loans to private sector enterprises, loans to any state-owned enterprise operating competitively, the question is that we have an appreciation of the operation, competitively, when it comes to determining whether a firm is able to apply and be a recipient of financing. Our view of operating competitively during this transition period, in terms of state owned enterprises, may be somewhat different from their own.
I submit that we ought to be as open as possible during this time to encourage, yes, a move to profitability when it makes sense, in terms of some of the state-owned enterprises but, again, to also recognize that the period
may be somewhat lengthy, that the transition may be somewhat longer than what we would tolerate in our own market-oriented economy and, that we must be willing to be flexible in terms of providing that kind of support.
Article 11 goes on, and I quote:
(iiXa) by investment in the equity capital of private sector enterprises;
(b)	by investment in the equity capital of any state-owned enterprise operating competitively-
And, again, Mr. Speaker, just in parenthesis, I want to add, once again, let us be open to the definition of competitiveness, particularly during this very difficult transition period in the central and eastern European countries and, particularly, the Soviet Union. I see, Mr. Speaker, you have a puzzled look on your face.
During this time when Mikhail Gorbachev is under a great deal of pressure, in terms of the successes or lack of successes of his initiative to perestroika, I think that anything we can do to facilitate the successful development of the Soviet economy, to provide assistance and to encourage power not to shift into the more conservative, military-aligned power base in the Soviet Union, would be not only an investment in our future as a western country but, indeed, in terms of the world itself, to do whatever we can to stand behind those progressive initiatives that, in very difficult times, he is attempting to introduce. I simply set that aside again from the comments on competitiveness of state-owned enterprises.
I want to go on because I believe it is important. We are talking about investment in the equity capital of any state-owned enterprise operating competitively and moving to participation in the market-oriented economy, the investment in the equity capital of any state-owned enterprise to facilitate its transition to private ownership and control, in particular, to facilitate or enhance the participation of private and/or foreign capital in such enterprises. And to go on, Mr. Speaker, the bill reads:
(c)	by underwriting, where other means of financing are not appropriate, the equity issue of securities by both private sector enterprises and such state-owned enterprises referred to above.
It is referring particularly to the state-owned enterprises operating competitively. This obviously is a critical part of Bill C-88.1 was going to refer to other sections of
January 21, 1991

the legislation. The continuation of Article 2, when it talks again of the purposes of this article, that state-owned enterprise shall not be regarded as operating competitively unless it operates autonomously in a competitive market environment, and unless it is subject to bankruptcy laws.
Again, it makes the point that during this difficult transition period when state-owned enterprises must operate competitively by operating autonomously and in a competitive market environment, that transition is not going to be an easy one. Therefore, it is in our best interest to assume these definitions very loosely.
I see this as an excellent opportunity for Canada to play a role in supporting and developing the eastern economies during this difficult transitional period.
There is much more, of course, that Canada could be doing. I do not have to tell members of Parliament that our aid and our support is required, not only in this part of the globe but, of course, in many other parts. I refer particularly to places such as Ethiopia, Sudan and areas of that part of Africa that are experiencing famine conditions where we ought to be doing, in my estimation, significantly more in not only alleviating the immediate concern in terms of hunger, but, of course, in terms of aid that will really assist those countries which would have to have us move away from some of the tied aid that we are involved with presently in not only that part of the world, but almost all parts.
In conclusion, I want to say that we support the general thrust of this bill with a number of very serious reservations. I do hope that the reservations of those who spoke before me, both in committee as well as in this debate, are considered by the government as we move to play our role in the hope of making it a most meaningful role in the economic reconstruction of eastern Europe, including the Soviet Union.
I would be remiss if I did not say that there are so many other ways that we can also be helpful, other than simply participating in this reconstruction bank. I look forward in the future to participating in those debates and in those committee discussions where in fact there will be wide ranging discussion of the future role of Canada in developing the economies of these countries.
