subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I congratulate you for having the wisdom to grant the House leave to debate this important crisis in one part of our world. I thank all parties and Independent members for agreeing to such an emergency debate on the crisis in the Baltic states.
Everyone thought that World War II ended on September 2 when the Japanese surrendered. Well, it didn't, because World War II continued. First, Hitler and Stalin occupied three countries under the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. With a stroke of a pen, they occupied three countries.
How does that differ from another country, such as Iraq, invading Kuwait? This one was done by military might, the other one was done by the stroke of a pen. In both cases, sovereign countries got their independence taken away. World War II continued, in a way, because the Baltic states did not accept that. Most of the western countries did not accept that annexation.
There were partisan military actions by Lithuanians and the others, hiding in the bushes, disrupting communications for the Soviet Union, and making life miserable for the Soviet army. But it did not stop there. It stopped for a period and then, of course, we saw the demonstrations. We actually saw 50 years of continuations of some aspects of World War II.
Then came the bloody crackdown a week ago in Vilnius, for no apparent reason. The reason, according to some sources, is because the young men refused to be conscripted into the army. Most of those men, I am sure, would welcome joining the army to defend their country, but not joining the Soviet Union to defend another country. If the Soviet Union Army orders these young men from the Baltic states to invade any of the Baltic states, they would be shooting at their own parents. They would be shooting at their own brothers and sisters. So I cannot blame the young men who are refusing to join the Soviet Army. They are very willing to join the Estonian, the Latvian, and the Lithuanian armies, but not the Soviet Army. This was not the real cause. I think, President Gorbachev or whoever gave the order to move in the tanks found that as an excuse.
What was the reaction around the world when Gorbachev decided to move tanks and troops into Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania? The reaction was swift and the reaction was strong from around the world.
At a meeting that the hon. member for Scarborough Centre and I had with about 500 Baltic Canadians on Saturday, they praised the Canadian government for acting so quickly. Canada was one of the first parliaments to bring in an all-party resolution condemning the actions of the Soviet Union in this crack-down.
But there was immediate reaction from the United States. The New York Times quotes President Bush as saying:
We condemn these acts which could not help but affect our
relationship-I ask the Soviet leaders to refrain from further acts that
January 21, 1991

might lead to more violence and loss of life. I urge the Soviet Government to return to a peaceful course of negotiations and dialogue with legitimate governments of the Baltic states.
Then, of course, this question came up: Should the summit between President Bush and President Gorbachev take place? I hope it is not cancelled, but postponed or suspended until such time as the Soviet Army is withdrawn from the Baltic states.
What was the reaction of the European Economic Community? The New York Times states:
The European Economic Community condemned Moscow's violent crackdown, warned that the $1 billion in economic aid promised to the Soviet Union might be suspended, and demanded an explanation from Moscow indicating which authorities ordered the troops to fire on unarmed civilians.
Then, country by country, they expressed their condemnation, but I will not have time to quote the condemnation of each country.
In eastern Europe, Czechoslovakia called for consultations with Poland and Hungary and stated that it foresaw the discussion of joint action, including withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact.
Just this weekend, I learned that the Government of Poland has accepted Lithuania's government, should it have to go into exile. Poland knows what it is like to achieve its independence. Lithuania, an independent country, should not have to fight for its independence. If, as a last resort, the Landsbergis government has to operate from outside of Lithuania, that government has been assured that there is spot for the government in exile in Warsaw. This is the kind of co-operation and reaction we are seeing from around the world.
Getting back to Canada's reaction, on January 9 I wrote a letter to the Secretary of State for External Affairs also asking that he condemn this action and that he call in the Soviet ambassador. I want to thank him now-I see him sitting here-that he did call in the ambassador to explain the actions of the Soviet Union.
The Prime Minister sent a letter to President Gorbachev warning President Gorbachev that unless such action stops, this may harm future relationships between our two countries. We all received press releases about that letter.
Of course, in the House we passed the all-party resolution. I must say that, when the hon. member for Edmonton Southeast, the hon. member for Scarborough East, and myself paid a visit to the Soviet ambassador, what seemed to irritate him the most was this all-party resolution.
The ambassador accused us of not being objective and fair, but we assured him that we were very objective and very fair, and that we will not stop our pressure and our actions until such time that the troops are withdrawn and until such time that the Soviet Union sits down and starts talking to the Baltic states.
We asked the ambassador, what is the bottom line? How can we get Lithuania, Estonia, and Latvia talking to the leadership of the Soviet Union? I was a little shocked to hear the ambassador go back almost to square one. His response was that they had a new constitution, so the first thing the Baltic states must do is hold a referendum. After the referendum, there will be a five-year waiting period with negotiations, et cetera. After five years, they might then might achieve their independence.
I throw in the word "might", because after five years there is still no guarantee that the Baltic states would actually achieve their independence.
When our external affairs committee was visiting the Soviet Union, the officials from the Soviet Union were trying to tell us that the Baltic states, if they want to secede, must pay back everything that the Soviet Union invested in the Baltic states, such as the infrastructure, et cetera.
I would say that the Baltic states are probably very willing to pay back anything the Soviet Union invested in the Baltic states, but, first, I think the Baltic states should present a bill to the Soviet Union and insist that the Soviet Union pay back everything that it raked from those three countries. Let them pay back the families that they sent to Siberia. Let them pay back for the families who did not return from Siberia. Let them pay back for the properties they stole from the Baltic people. I am sure they would find that they owe more to the Baltic states than the Baltic states owe the Soviet Union. To me, that is an argument.
During any talks that we have had with representatives from the Baltic states, including President Landsbergis,

January 21, 1991
President Godmanis, and all the representatives who were here from Estonia, they said: "We want nothing more than to sit down with the Soviet Union representatives to negotiate a peaceful settlement."
Being in Lithuania for the free elections on February 24,1 do not think we could find a more peaceful people, with peace as their whole attitude, than the people of the Baltic states. They do not want war. They want to settle this peacefully, but no one is talking to them because they keep going back to the line: We have a constitution. They must secede following the constitution. The elections of February 24 were held prior to the constitution being adopted.
On the referendum issue, the Baltic states are asking why they should have to hold a referendum asking people whether they want independence. They have been independent countries all along. By agreeing to a referendum, they would be telling the Soviet Union and the world that they are not independent. This is like asking Canadians to have a referendum on whether we are a sovereign, independent nation.
This is where the two sides seem to be hung up. Maybe this is where Canada can play a vital role in trying to get the two sides together to try to break this stalemate. The Soviet Union will not talk until the Baltic states hold their referendums. The Baltic states say recognize us as independent countries and let us negotiate. There is a big role here, perhaps, for Canada to play.
I am trying to explain why the stalemate. Anyone we talked to, whether it was in the Soviet Union, with the external affairs committee or representatives coming here, the message we got was that the governments of the Baltic states want to negotiate.
The other thing of which I might just remind President Gorbachev is that I did not see the elections in Estonia and Latvia but I witnessed the election in Lithuania. Is that not a referendum, when people elect their own Parliaments, when every party, and every independent candidate can run in the election? The people have spoken. They have elected their own democratic Parliaments. How can the Soviet Union now try to take those freely elected Parliaments away from them? This is what it is trying to do in Lithuania and, this weekend, in Latvia and next weekend, I hope it is not Estonia. But because the world is speaking up, let us hope the Soviet Union
will not attempt the same scenario in Estonia. The way it is going, it seems that that is its strategy, next weekend Estonia, two weekends from now back to Lithuania and Latvia and repeat the whole cycle. I hope that is not its strategy.
In meeting with the Baltic community, our parliamentary group on the Baltic states, has been getting very clear messages as to what the Baltic Canadian communities want. I am not saying this, Mr. Speaker, this is from the Lithuanian-Canadian community which asks the Canadian government to take the following actions in the wake of the brutal crackdown in Vilnius by the Soviet army: (1) impose sanctions on the U.S.S.R. until it withdraws its tanks and paratroopers from Vilnius and enters into negotiations with the legitimate Government of Lithuania; (2) immediately accord diplomatic recognition to the democratically-elected Government of the Republic of Lithuania, led by President Vytautus Lands-bergis; (3) introduce a Canadian resolution in the United Nations condemning the Soviet aggression and to push for an emergency meeting of the UN Security Council in order to debate the Baltic crisis; and, (4) call a special meeting of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe to condemn the assault on Lithuania as a threat to the peace of Europe. That came from the Lithuanian community.
And this weekend, in the meeting we had, the Latvian community put forward four proposals that it would like our Parliament to address. It calls upon the Canadian government to: (1) immediately cease all assistance to the Soviet Union and impose trade and economic sanctions; (2) call an emergency debate in the House of Commons. We met that request, that is what we are doing tonight. The third proposal was: to call on the United Nations to send observers to the Baltic states. I would like to enlarge upon that one. The Baltic Canadians were saying that they wanted the United Nations to send observers but they were saying that they would also like this Parliament to send Canadian observers. They had the experience of having Canadian observers over there before and they are requesting that our government send Canadian observers to observe what is going on now. Their feeling is that if there are international observers now Gorbachev will think twice before flying in the Black Beret paratroopers. Fourth, continue to raise the Baltic issue at the Conference on Security and
January 21, 1991

Co-operation in Europe by stressing that Soviet actions will continue to threaten the peace of Europe until democracy is restored.
The Estonian community makes the same requests. If you look at the requests from the Lithuanian and Latvian community, the Estonian community requests would be quite similar.
Thank you again, Mr. Speaker, for allowing us to have this emergency debate. I said this before and I will say it again in this House: there are two crises facing us, one is the Iraqi crisis, the other is the Baltic crisis. The world rejoiced when the cold war came to an end. Let us remember how much money was wasted on arms because of the cold war. Now we can save that money and put it toward feeding the poor, providing better housing for our people. If this crisis is not settled, we are going to go back to another cold war period where east and west are going to be building up arms, east and west will stop trading with each other and stop talking with each other.
Mr. Speaker, no one in this Parliament, or in any parliament around the world would want this.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Chair for having allowed this debate to take place. As well I would like to thank the member for Parkdale-High Park and the member for Winnipeg Transcona for raising this important issue in this House. I think it is an all-party issue.
The Prime Minister of Canada on January 13 sent a strong message to Mr. Gorbachev to live up to his promise of opening the Soviet society, and opening the Soviet society to the world.
I would like first to quote what was written about the tough line of Mr. Gorbachev on republic sovereignty in The Globe and Mail of December 10. I quote:
Was it only coincidence that Soviet authorities chose to crush the
1956 Hungarian uprising while the Western world was preoccupied
with the Suez crisis; or that Stalin sent his tanks into the Baltic states
the day the Nazis marched into Paris?
He doesn't think so. Nor does he believe it is a mere coincidence that while the rest of the world focuses on the potential war in the Persian Gulf, Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev appears to be preparing to crush the
independent movement in the Baltic and other Soviet republics.
I think what is happening today is a tragedy. This is the anxiety that Canadians and people elsewhere in the world have today. If you look at the development in the Persian Gulf, the American Armed Forces have over
450,000	people there. They have withdrawn armed forces from Europe and from elsewhere to send to the Persian Gulf. During that period the Soviet Union is cracking down on the Soviet republics in the Baltics.
I have been to the Soviet Union on five occasions. When I was there in the fall of 1989, I could see that changes were beginning to occur. The Soviet Union was opening up. They were debating the market economy, having democratic elections and so on and so forth.
What is happening now? It seems that the hardliners are slowly taking over in the Soviet Union. Mr. Gorbachev seems to be acting on somebody else's behalf.
Coming back to 1989, when I was returning from the Soviet Union, while stopped in Vienna, I picked up a German newspaper. In that paper I read that the Archbishop of Austria was telling the Austrians and the world to pray for Mr. Gorbachev because he was the man who was opening the Soviet society to the world. They had acknowledged the atrocities that had been committed by Stalin during the 1930s against the Baltic nations. That archbishop was telling the world to pray for Mr. Gorbachev.
We saw during the period that followed the opening of the Soviet Union to the world. The Soviet Union allowed the unification of West Germany with East Germany. They allowed a democratic process in Czechoslovakia and Hungary. There was a spill-over effect into Yugoslavia where they were having free elections in Croatia, in Bosnia-Herzogovina and other parts of Yugoslavia.
We saw what happened to the regime in Romania. All this was as a consequence of Mr. Gorbachev's actions.
I went back to the Soviet Union just last year, again in the fall. I was amazed by the openness that was prevailing, especially in the Ukraine and Baltic states. They had had democratic elections. People were talking about the market economy. I had the pleasure and honour to speak to a regional parliament in the Ukraine. It was like here, everybody was able to express themselves. At the same time, other phenomena were occurring. There were

January 21, 1991
shortages of food and other commodities in the Soviet Union and in the Baltic states.
My understanding is that the conservative forces, conservative in the sense of those who wanted to maintain the old regime, were sabotaging the reforms of the progressive people who were surrounding Mr. Gorbachev. You could almost feel that if help was not forthcoming from the west, the conservative forces in the Soviet Union, the communist forces, would take over. I am afraid that this is what is slowly happening. The intentions were excellent. We have to pay tribute to Mr. Gorbachev to have wanted something to happen but, at the same time, people like Mr. Yeltsin are already saying other forces are at work.
I would like to quote from The Ottawa Citizen of today. An address from Mr. Yeltsin was read to 300,000 people in Moscow who were supporting the democratic process. Mr. Boris Yeltsin warned of dictatorship unfolding in Russia. When he talks about Russia, he talks about the Soviet imperialist powers. He is not talking about Russia itself, because Mr. Yeltsin is the President of Russia. He is not the President of the Soviet Union and he was elected with a huge majority. He warns of the dictatorship unfolding in Russia, if the public does not rise against growing signs that the Kremlin is in the grip of conservative communists.
Economic reforms have been blocked, democracy betrayed, and glasnost trampled upon. This is about what Mr. Yeltsin is warning the world. Mr. Shevardnadze has done the same. He has resigned because he felt dictatorship is coming back to the Soviet Union.
As we watch the happenings in the Middle East, as we watch how people are being destroyed in this war on both sides, and as all our attention is focused on the Middle East, as I said at the beginning, very profound changes are happening in the Soviet Union.
We could ask ourselves the question: Why did the Soviet Union co-operate with the United Nations? Normally it would have vetoed any action by the United States and other countries in the Persian Gulf, but it wants the world's attention to focus on the Middle East as the armed forces of the United States are involved in
a long and difficult war. It is in a sense that those conservative forces in the Soviet Union, the old time communists, are probably happy with what is happening in the Middle East because they can take over.
What is happening right now in Lithuania, Estonia, and Latvia is a tragedy because those countries were given away, as the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park said, by signatures on a piece of paper by Hitler and Stalin. It was a deal.
I hope that there was no deal between the United States and the Soviet Union in the Middle East, what we call the new world order: your sphere of influence is going to be the Middle East and our sphere of influence is going to be eastern Europe. I am sure Mr. Gorbachev had very good intentions, but he is no longer in control of what is happening in the Soviet Union.
I would like to mention that this crackdown is not only taking place in the Baltic states. In the Ukraine as well, members of Parliament are being arrested in the Parliament Buildings. One of those is Mr. Khmara. I would like to read a short letter that I wrote to the Prime Minister on December 13. This message was delivered in Toronto to a gathering of people who were fighting for Mr. Khmara's liberation from jail:
I wish to join those present here today to express our concern about what is happening in the Ukraine.
As we know, Mr. Khmara is a member of the Ukrainian Parliament, a leading human rights advocate, a former prisoner of conscience, and founding member of the Helsinki Human Rights Movement. He has been arrested on drummed-up charges by the secret police of the central government.
That is the Kremlin. It continues:
I hope that this is not a change in policy by Moscow.
Recently, we have seen serious clouds develop on the horizon of glasnost. The appointment of Mr. Boris Pugo, a hardline KGB major-general from Latvia, as Interior Minister of the Soviet Socialist Republics, indicates that there is a move towards a hardline position and away from democratization of Soviet society.
I ask the Prime Minister to tell Mr. Gorbachev that Canadians will not support flagrant human rights violations, as in the case of Mr. Khmara.
We should never abandon the fight for human rights, wherever they occur.
Those changes that are taking place in the Soviet Union are more dramatic in the Baltic states. I support
January 21, 1991

the request by the Lithuanian Canadian community that sent a letter to most members of Parliament. One of the actions that the Secretary of State of External Affairs and the Prime Minister should take immediately is to accord diplomatic recognition to the democratically elected government of the Republic of Lithuania, led by President Landsbergis, and those of Latvia and Estonia as well. I think this is the minimum that the Canadian government can do.
I would like to thank all members who want to participate in the debate. I feel that changes in the Soviet Union were certainly very positive until lately. Now we have to remind the leaders in the Kremlin that the world cannot watch the process of glasnost stop.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is not very often unanimity in this House, even on questions of international policy, but I think that this is one of those occasions in which the House of Commons of Canada speaks, if not with one voice, then certainly with one purpose and one conviction, and that is to send the clearest possible signal to the leadership of the Soviet Union and to the Baltic peoples that Canada, each and every one of us, each and every Canadian, opposes absolutely the crackdown that has begun to develop in the Soviet Union against aspirations and governments which have a legitimacy in the Baltic states.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The hard question for us, and one that I think we cannot answer tonight, is what exactly and practically the people and Government of Canada can do to reverse these developments. We are all determined to seek the reversal and to find ways that are available to us within the limits we face as a government with obligations and restrictions in the family of nations.
Everyone, every Canadian, I believe, is shocked by the brutal and unwarranted use of military force against the people and democratically elected governments of the Baltic states last week in Lithuania and yesterday in Riga, Latvia. We condemn such appalling and reprehensible behaviour, and we call upon Soviet President Gorbachev to do the same.
No one can remain unmoved by the vigilant and peaceful struggle of the peoples of the Baltic states to regain their independence. Their future is bound up in that of the new international order we are trying to create, whether that is in Europe or in the gulf.
For that reason this debate is important. It is important also to make it clear to the leaders of the Soviet Union that whatever our preoccupations with a war in which Canadian lives are at stake in the gulf, those preoccupations will not allow anyone to get away with a crackdown of the kind that is beginning, that is all too evident now in the Baltic states.
I want to commend the excellent work of the member for Scarborough Centre who presides over an ad hoc committee of members of Parliament on the Baltic states. They have been concerned, committed, and tireless in their efforts on behalf of the Canadian Baltic communities and the people who come from there.
Canada's support for the Baltic states has been unwavering. We recognize their de jure independence. We have never accepted their forcible annexation. We support the right of their peoples to determine their own future. The question for us is what practical help can we offer now.
I have just had the great privilege of meeting, in my capacity as a parliamentarian, with Vice-President Ivans of Latvia who came up particularly to see me tonight and is going now for meetings later this evening or early tomorrow morning with the Secretary of State of the United States. We talked about three areas in which the help of Canada can be offered: one is material, one is moral and political, and the third is diplomatic.
Regarding material help, there may well be in Latvia, as there sadly is in Lithuania, a need for some medical supplies. I asked Vice-President Ivans, on behalf of the government and people of Canada, to prepare a list of the things that might be needed by the Latvian people, things that we might be in a position to provide, and we would then look at ways-and they could be difficult-by which those might be delivered to people in need.
I would encourage groups in Canada who might have materials, medical supplies, perhaps other things, that would be necessary to consider ways by which those

January 21, 1991
might be gathered and made available for transmission to people in the Baltic states.
In terms of moral and political support, two or three matters were raised by the Vice-President of Latvia. One of them I think must be considered carefully by this House. It holds some risks, including personal risks and including a risk of being counterproductive, and that is the possibility of a delegation of parliamentarians of this House going to Latvia.
As Secretary of State for External Affairs I would not at the moment make a recommendation on that matter. I think that is simply because this debate comes so quickly after the proposal was made.
There are some positive things that could be gained from a gesture of that kind. But there are dangers, some of them personal in the circumstances, and also the danger that that kind of action by parliamentarians from this House would invite exactly the opposite response from what we seek from the Soviet Union.
The Baltic countries have established a Baltic centre in Stockholm. That is something the Government of Sweden has determined to be acceptable by its interpretation of international law and practice. Certainly I think it is important and useful for us to consider whether a similar arrangement might be applied here.
There are things that we have to consider doing on the diplomatic front, as was discussed in this House in answer to questions from my friend for Winnipeg Trans-cona. There has to be consideration as to what we can do in the context of the United Nations, probably most likely in its committees dealing with human rights. We are already trying to define some ways in which we can make progress through the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. I want to return to that theme a little bit later tonight.
As the two speakers preceding me have indicated, what is happening in Latvia and Lithuania is inseparable from the broader situation in the Soviet Union, a situation which becomes more troubling every day, particularly for those of us who were so encouraged by the movement towards glasnost and perestroika and so determined to do what we can to help those reforms succeed.
None of us wants the Soviet Union to crumble. All of us want reform in that society to succeed. We were
encouraged, among other things, by the attitudes that had been shown generally earlier with respect to the status of the Baltic states. We are discouraged now, deeply discouraged, by actions that have become more violent and more dramatic in recent days.
There are things we must consider doing to support the Baltic people, but we must try to do them in the context of encouraging the reform and the cohesion of the Soviet Union. That is a particularly difficult challenge for all of us, but it is, I think, Mr. Speaker, in everybody's interest, including the interest of the people in the Baltic states and the people of Baltic origin in Canada, that we seek a way that accomplishes or encourages together the reform that was started by Mr. Gorbachev in the Soviet Union and some movement towards the independence of the Baltic states.
There is no clear way, at least not clear to me, in which we can accomplish that goal tonight. But the Soviet Union, as it considers what it is doing now, and as it considers the importance to it of the support of a people and a government like ours, must understand that Canadians not only have commitments to human rights that are so much a part of our society, but also have a population that was formed in such large part by people who came from eastern and central Europe and from communities in what is now the Soviet Union.
Canadians cannot help but be profoundly affected by what is occurring in the Soviet Union now, and that if those actions do not stop, they are bound to have an effect for the worse upon the relations between Canada and the Soviet Union in a formal sense, but also, and perhaps in a much more important way, they are bound to dim and then to reverse the enthusiasm for reform that had been building among our own people, most particularly among people who had roots behind what used to be the Iron Curtain.

Canada's support for the Baltic states has been unwavering. We recognize their independence by right. We never accepted their annexation by force. We argue in favour of the right of these peoples to determine their future.
Last spring, the three republics held fair and free elections. Federal representatives, including the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park, the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona and the hon. member for Scarbo-
January 21, 1991

rough Centre, and a representative from Ontario, Premier Rae, went to Lithuania during the election as observers.
At the initiative of Lithuania, on March 11, these democratically-elected governments declared their independence from the U.S.S.R. They tried to negotiate with Moscow, as provided under the existing constitution. Instead they were subjected to political and economic pressure.
After five years of a steadily deteriorating standard of living, perestroika has now reached a critical phase. The Soviet economy is crumbling. Pressure from independence movements is rising and public opinion is becoming increasingly negative. Mr. Gorbachev must choose: advance or retreat.
Gorbachev's supporters claim that law and order are the only weapons against anarchy. His opponents say that a policy of oppression will make him the hostage of reactionary forces. Polarization quickly leads to instability-
This winter, the U.S.S.R. asked Canada and other Western countries for assistance. We decided to support reforms by reducing the cost of transition. After my conversations with the former minister of foreign affairs, Mr. Shevardnadze, the Prime Minister of Canada offered specific types of assistance at the last CSCE summit in Paris. All of this is now at risk.

That things were getting worse in the Soviet Union was evident when Mr. Shevardnadze resigned in mid-December, warning that dictatorship could be on the way. The tragic events in Vilnius the night of January 12-13, with 14 dead, 163 wounded and 57 missing, made Mr. Shevardnadze, unhappily, a prophet. Mr. Gorbachev has taken the position that the events in Vilnius were regrettable but inevitable. He has not condemned the violence; he has not expressed sympathy for the victims or repudiated those who ordered it. His ultimatum to the Baltic states gave the military a green light, though he is disclaiming any personal knowledge of the consequences.
All three Baltic states believe that military-enforced, direct presidential rule is imminent. They are directing urgent appeals to Canada and to other western states,
making an explicit linkage to the gulf crisis. The three have sent out representatives empowered to establish governments in exile if required. And, as the House knows and as I have said, I met earlier this evening with the Vice-President of Latvia.
Making any assessment difficult is the lack of coherence in Moscow among the various constituencies vying for power. Russian Republic President Yeltsin has joined the Baltic states in opposing the centre. Tens of thousands of people demonstrated in Moscow yesterday, calling for Mr. Gorbachev's resignation and the restoration of democracy. Meanwhile, the situation in other republics is increasingly tense, in Georgia, in Armenia, in Moldavia and in Ukraine. Mr. Gorbachev and the military have threatened them with similar treatment if they do not knuckle under. Many believe that the Baltic states are the dress rehearsal.
Last spring, Canada welcomed the free elections in the Baltic states, stressing our support for the right of their peoples to determine their own future. We protested the Soviet resort to intimidation. In my parliamentary capacity, I met with the then Prime Minister of Lithuania, Madam Prunskiene. Canada moved quickly to express its concern about the dangerous situation currently developing in the Baltic states. In December, the Prime Minister and I, in our parliamentary capacities, met with Lithuanian President Landsbergis, Latvian Prime Minister Godmanis and Foreign Minister Jurkans. I wrote to former foreign minister Shevardnadze on December 13 seeking confirmation of explicit assurances that were given to me and to the Prime Minister a year ago that there would be no crackdown in the Baltic states. On January 8 and January 11, the Soviet ambassador was called in.
I, on behalf of the Government of Canada, issued tough statements. Canada's reaction to the tragic events in Vilnius was among the strongest to come from any democracy in the western world.
The Prime Minister wrote immediately to President Gorbachev. He issued a strong condemnation, calling on the Soviet President to show restraint and to negotiate settlements based on the Helsinki Final Act and the Charter of Paris. He reminded him that at this time of heightened international tension, Canadians were watching events in the U.S.S.R. just as we were watching events in the gulf.

At the same time, the Prime Minister announced that Canada was reviewing its offer of technical assistance and the new $150 million line of credit. That is not food aid, but a commercial sale. We have drawn a direct linkage between Canadian assistance and the continuation of Soviet reform. I announced earlier that we were reviewing actions under those programs. I want to advise the House that we have now suspended any action under those programs that had not taken place before the actions in Lithuania.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
On January 15, this House passed a unanimous resolution condemning the brutal violence used against the people and democratically elected Government of Lithuania.
Saturday I received a communication from the Soviet Ambassador giving the official explanation for the tragic events in Lithuania. The note rejected Moscow's responsibility for what happened, blaming instead the Lithuanian leaders who were claimed to have held extremist positions. That, however, was before the equally tragic events in Riga yesterday.
No one knows if Mr. Gorbachev is still in charge or, more worrying, whether he remains committed to the reforms that began in his name. In his letter of January 13, the Prime Minister warned the Soviet President against the consequences of his present course. That letter remains unanswered, and tonight I would like to quote it and lay it on the table of Parliament.

The Prime Minister wrote:
Dear Mr. President,
I am writing to express the shock and abhorrence felt by all Canadians at the unwarranted violence used against the people and democratically elected government of Lithuania.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs raised Canada's concerns with the Soviet Ambassador, January 11. Since then, Soviet military forces have been used against the institutions and citizens of Lithuania with resulting serious injuries and loss of life.
I deeply regret that these actions have taken place. They are contrary to the assurances Mr. Clark had received from Foreign Minister Shevardnadze and which you had explicitly repeated to me that there would be no crackdown in the Baltic states. I cannot stress to
you strongly enough the importance of quickly and unequivocally condemning such behaviour.
You have accomplished a great deal in bringing new hope to your nation and the world. I appeal to you not to undermine this achievement but to show restraint in this increasingly dangerous situation so that further bloodshed can be averted. I urge you to seek negotiated solutions consistent with the Helsinki Final Act, the Charter of Paris and the legitimate aspirations of Lithuania and the other Baltic States. Democracy cannot exist without respect for fundamental human rights and freedoms.
As of now, Canada is reviewing its offers of technical assistance and new lines of credit for the purchase of foodstuffs. Developments in the Baltic States will also have an impact on the agreements reached during Mr. Clark's visit to Moscow and in our discussions at the CSCE Paris Summit.
I must stress that further escalation will have serious consequences for our relations. As Mr. Clark advised the Soviet Ambassador, at this time of heightened international tension, we are watching events not only in the Gulf, but in the USSR as well. In circumstances such as these, you should not underestimate the force of Canadian and world opinion.
That was the Prime Minister's letter to Mr. Gorbatch-ev, and I am prepared to lay it on the Thble of the House.

I understand that I am close to the end of my allotted time. I wonder if I might have two or three minutes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, officials of the Departments of External Affairs and International Trade are in continuous contact with representatives of the Baltic communities and concerned individuals.
For example, we are continuing to facilitate the shipment of medical supplies to Lithuania and to other Baltic states.
In Moscow, our embassy has been repeating Canada's message, the message of the House of Commons and our government, to the Soviets through the ministry of foreign affairs there, including a conversation today between Ambassador Michael Bell of Canada and the
new Foreign Minister Bessmertnykh of the Soviet Union.
An embassy officer is on the ground in Vilnius providing consular services to Canadians in the region and acting as a channel of communication. He is in direct contact with President Landsbergis.
Another embassy officer is leaving for Riga shortly.
We are looking at ways of including the Baltic States in the CSCE process. Canada is making strong statements at the CSCE conference in Valetta, the meeting on the peaceful resolution of disputes, and will do the same at ongoing meetings in Vienna.
Canada and others will be invoking the human dimension mechanism of the CSCE, which we think may provide us more influence than we had heretofore seeking explanations formally from Soviet authorities about what is happening in the Baltic states.
As the House knows, the member from Markham raised a proposal in the House today of which I have taken note regarding the conference under the CSCE process on human rights.
We are discussing the situation with our allies in NATO and are considering the means by which it might be raised effectively in the United Nations, especially in the Commission on Human Rights meeting in Geneva later this month. Members of Parliament have made the point to me that, while they understand the effect of the veto on matters that might be raised in the Security Council, the presence of that veto should not in and of itself preclude us from raising the matter either there or in the General Assembly. We are looking at ways effect can be given to that view.
Bilaterally, we are looking at concrete ways that Canada can support the Baltic states through increased contacts and direct assistance. We are also exploring with the Baltic communities in Canada the possibilities of opening a Baltic information office here in Canada.
I am prepared to look at any other ways that are practical. There are limits upon what we can do, given our obligations in the family of nations and given the importance of our continuing relations with the Soviet Union, given the importance indeed of our capacity to influence that country and that government, not simply in matters it considers internal but also in other international matters.

January 21, 1991
I can say that, while I am aware of those limits, it is my intention and the personal commitment of the Prime Minister to push those limits as far as is humanly possible. I will need not simply the support of the House in that, but also the advice of the House as to means that might be followed that can accomplish that purpose. Any proposals that are put forward in this debate or later will be seriously considered.
The purpose of this debate, I believe, is to make one message clear to the Baltic peoples, and most particularly to the leadership in the Soviet Union, and that is that the violence and repression that we have seen in recent days is completely unacceptable to Canada, unacceptable to this Parliament, and poses a grave risk to relations that we want to pursue and to reforms that we want to encourage in the Soviet Union.
There is a crisis in the gulf that preoccupies us all. If leaders of the Soviet Union thought that would deflect the attention of Canadians, this Parliament, or this government away from the situation of the Baltic peoples, then they were wrong. We are committed to support principles that have been important to Canadians for years and to support peoples whose braveiy and determination have won the admiration of all of us.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the right hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs for his speech, and also the two co-sponsors of the motion to bring on this emergency debate, the existence of which I think sends an important signal, particularly to the Soviet Union, about the seriousness
with which the Canadian Parliament takes recent events in Latvia and Lithuania. Also, it sends a signal to the Baltic community within Canada as to how serious the Canadian Parliament takes events in Lithuania and Latvia, and the concern which the Baltic community in Canada rightly has about their countries of origin.
I was going to say, while I have the secretary of state's attention, that I will send over to him a fax which I received indirectly over the weekend from the Minister of Health in Lithuania, Mr. Juozaz Oleksas. I stayed in his home for 10 days when I was in Lithuania observing the elections. It is a rather detailed piece of information about the nature of the violence, the wounds that people received, causes of death, et cetera, and an extensive list of the kinds of medical supplies which are in short supply. I send that over to him now. It may be in the file at External Affairs, but just in case he does not have it already, he will have it now.
With respect to the emergency debate, it is one of a number of steps that have already been taken by this Parliament with respect to the situation in Lithuania and Latvia, going all the way back to March of last year when we passed a resolution recognizing the right-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I say I would rather not talk over the voices of people on the other side. This is an emergency debate. There is an emergency in Latvia and Lithuania and, if members are going to be in the Chamber, they can at least pay attention to what is going on or have their conversations somewhere else.
With respect to what the Canadian Parliament has done so far, I was taking you back, Mr. Speaker, to the passage of the resolution in March, 1990 by which we recognized, collectively, the right of the Baltic states to declare their independence and the resolution of January 15, 1991 in which we called upon the Soviet Union, given what had already happened in Lithuania on the previous weekend, to stop the violence which was being visited upon civilians. Now, of course, there is the situation in Latvia where, again, people have been killed by the military, the so-called Black Berets.
I am very pleased to be part of this collective effort on the part of Canadian parliamentarians, an effort which owes its existence to a consensus about the situation in
January 21, 1991

the Baltic, but also I think to the actions of the group known as the Canadian Parliamentary Group for the Baltic Peoples. That group has its origin in the visit of Canadian parliamentarians to Lithuania in February 1990 in order to observe the elections there which brought to power, so to speak, the Sajudis Party. Sajudis is an umbrella movement which contains within it various ideological factions from Greens to social democrats, communists, Christian democrats, and a variety of people who were united in one thing and that was to see the day when Lithuania would regain the independence that it once enjoyed as a sovereign state.
I remember only too well the experience that I had there. We were of course in Vilnius for most of the time we were there, but one evening-I believe it was on a Friday night-I went to a small town near the Baltic Sea called Silute in which I was able to attend a town hall meeting where there were a variety of candidates. I think there were six candidates in all running in that particular riding. They had a town hall meeting at which the candidates spoke and there was a question and answer period after. Of course, because I was a guest, I got to say why I was there. I was also invited to say a word at the end of the meeting.
One of the things that I had to say was that it was the most polite, most civil, and most profound town hall meeting I had ever been at. It made all the town hall meeting that I had experienced as a Canadian politician look rather inferior. Perhaps because people realized the stakes, I think, of what they were arguing about and what they were debating, they were very generous with each other.
I reflected at that time that perhaps we take democracy too much for granted in this country and abuse, in many respects, our freedom of speech by being unkind to each other in ways that are not called for. These people knew the value of what they were experiencing for the first time in 50 years and treated it with a great deal of care.
Of course, the other side of that coin is that their politics have not yet come to be trivialized in the way that our politics has come to be trivialized by the media, the sound bite, negative advertising, and all the other things that afflict the body politic in western democracies.
Having said that, it is one of the things-the experience of that night and other experiences that I had there-that continues to motivate me in keeping what is happening in the Baltic states on the agenda of Parliament and on the international agenda, to the extent that any one member of Parliament can effect these things. I saw there, and I think we continue to see, a determination on the part of Lithuanians-although they are willing to defend themselves if pushed-to do what they have done so far in a very peaceful and democratic way, and in a very courageous way I might add.
We say to the Soviet Union, I hope, by everything we do and say here today, that we want the existence of those democratically elected governments of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania to be preserved, to be preserved not just all holed up in the parliament buildings somewhere, under siege, but to be preserved as a legitimate instrument by which the eventual independence or new relationship, whatever it comes to be with Moscow, can be negotiated. Let Moscow or the centralized authority in the Soviet Union negotiate as toughly as it wishes in a democratic way about the consequences of independence in the same way that any other country would want to negotiate toughly and realistically with parts of it that wanted to seek sovereignty. I do not need to make any obvious comparisons.
Those governments have been elected in fair and democratic elections. For me, that is the bottom line of continuing goodwill toward the Soviet Union, that those democratically elected governments not be overthrown or replaced with non-elected governments. There are plenty of difficult issues to be sorted out between those elected governments and Moscow. There are plenty of difficult questions regarding security, respect for ethnic minorities in the Baltic republics and questions having to do with what the terms of separation would be and so on. These are things that will take time.
To that extent, it is incumbent upon the leadership in the various Baltic republics to understand the over-all difficulty of the situation in the Soviet Union and to proceed in a way that is tactically wise and that takes into account those realities. I am not in a position to judge whether they have done that or not, but we are all in a position to say that that is something they need to take into account.

I met with the Soviet ambassador on Friday before I returned to my riding and received what we have received before in terms of an official explanation from the Soviet Union. That is the explanation that the external affairs committee got when we were in Moscow in April 1990, that there is a provision for the separation of republics from the Soviet Union. It is a five-year process and it is something that they ask the Baltic republics to respect.
The problem is twofold: One, for the Baltic republics to accept that constitutionalized process for separation is for them to accept the Soviet constitution. They are not willing to do this because they maintain that they have a special status, recognized by a significant part of the international community which never recognized their annexation by the Soviet Union. For them to seek separation purely and only within this established constitutional process is to concede the point on which they base their entire political self-understanding.
The second thing which is never highlighted by Soviet spokespersons, unless you ask them, is that at the end of this five-year process, any separation, even if it is ratified by referendum-and I think I am correct in this understanding-still has to be approved by Moscow. There is a sort of a trump card at the end which the Lithuanians and others suspect would be used against them. There are problems there.
What is needed is for the Baltic leadership to recognize the difficulty which the Soviet Union finds itself in, at the same time as Moscow recognizes the special case of the Baltics. This special case is established in the report by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade in our report on our visit there. It is not a new thought but one which I think still has to be fully absorbed by the Soviet Union, the extent to which the special case of the Baltics is something that it would be wise for a variety of ways for the Soviet Union to accept and not only because it would permit it to negotiate with the leadership in the Baltic republics at this point.
If they were able to establish a different relationship with the Baltic republics and permit a transition to a market economy, for instance, in the Baltics quicker than they are obviously able to do it elsewhere, they
might in a way have sort of a pilot project for perestroika. Things might be able to happen more quickly, more easily and provide the basis for the kind of change that needs to take place in other parts of the Soviet Union.
Obviously, this is an argument that has not been accepted by the Soviet leadership, but I think it is something that does recommend itself. I am very sorry that those arguments have not been heard or, at least, have not been accepted in Moscow or at the Kremlin. I do not disagree with the decision that the minister has announced to suspend various things that were in train with respect to the Soviet Union, but I regret very much that it has come to that as I am sure the minister of external affairs does.
I think this new relationship with the Soviet Union that was and still is developing is not only important for Canada because the Soviet Union happens to be one of our largest neighbours in every respect but also because the new relationship that the whole world was entering into with the Soviet Union is very important to the future of the planet for obvious reasons.
The point of the Secretary of State for External Affairs is well taken when he says that we have to judge how we respond to these events in light of the whole context of our relationship with the Soviet Union. That involves some very difficult decisions, because it is quite understandable that the community here in Canada has a list of the things that it would like the government to do.
I think we should be able, even though we share these concerns, to disagree with each other on a tactical level as to what will achieve the desired result and what may have to be held back at this point in order to preserve larger possibilities within which the possibility for an independent Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia is contained.
I believe that if the Soviet Union were to crumble-to use the minister's words-or were seen to be crumbling, that this would provide the opportunity for the army in the Soviet Union, at least in the short term, to take over, to exert more influence and to perpetrate more of the kind of violence that we have seen in Latvia and Lithuania.
I think there are some very difficult judgments to be made there and I hope that we all, as politicians, have the understanding of the various communities when we try to be as serious as we can about this and not just
January 21, 1991

simply agree with people for the sake of achieving political points.
With respect to the gulf, I am not sure. I have a suspicious enough mind growing out of my life in politics to believe that all kinds of things are not coincidence, but I think it is fair to say that the gulf war does distract attention from the events in the Baltics. Whether this was deliberate or not is really almost beside the point.
I think things would have come to a head there anyway in the absence of any willingness on the part of Moscow to accept the special case of the Baltics. Whether we were dealing with this now or later, we probably would have been dealing with it at some time. But it does raise some interesting questions vis-a-vis the gulf because here we are all agreeing, and yet over the gulf we cannot seem to agree.
It would be useful it seems to me to try to find what it is in the government's position with respect to the gulf that might permit it new freedom of action with respect to Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia; that is, this new emphasis on the United Nations which the government-I believe sincerely even though I disagree-sees as the underpinning of its action with respect to the gulf.
I think here is another opportunity for the UN to exercise itself on a situation which is entirely new, in the sense that it is not even a year since we have had these new democratically elected governments. It is entirely new in the sense that this is the post-1989 post-cold war world that we are dealing with.
I do not agree with the way in which this post-cold war United Nations has dealt with the gulf, but I think that this is another situation which asks of this new United Nations, which asks of this new post-cold war order, how shall we deal with this?
In that sense, new thinking has to be applied to that situation as well. Nothing in the way that we have dealt with these questions before is a truly reliable guidepost for us. I think some of the new thinking that has gone into the United Nations by the Soviet Union in some of the speeches by the now resigned foreign minister Eduard Shevardnadze need to be examined for ways in which the Soviet Union can be taken at its own word on how to deal with the situation in the Baltic republics.
I would commend that analytical task, if you like, to the minister and to the department because it may be that in things which have been said over the last little while by the Soviet Union you may find the hook by which to persuade them that they have an obligation, consistent with their own rhetoric to allow the Baltic situation to be debated at the UN; or considered by the Security Council; or whatever the case may be.
The object of all these things is to get the issue of the Baltic states into the international arena where it properly belongs, as a result of the longstanding contention by the international community, that the annexation of the Baltic states is only a de facto reality and not the the de jure reality that would enable the Soviet Union to claim that this was purely an internal matter, which raises, Mr. Speaker-

The point we need to look at-after the gulf war is over-hopefully soon-is how do we so reform the United Nations to enable it to legitimately concern itself with what nations regard as their internal affairs?
We can no longer go on like this permitting government after government, whether it is Canada with respect to native rights; the Soviet Union with respect to Lithuania; to Iraq, with respect to the Kurds; or whoever it happens to be, to claim that this is purely an internal matter. I think that is an agenda for reform that the government should turn its attention to.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be brief. I want to first of all congratulate my colleague for his very insightful analysis of the situation in the Baltic republics. I know that he has travelled to that area himself, specifically to the Baltic republics, and last year he was in the Soviet Union as well. Certainly he has been one of the leaders in this House on this very important question.
As the spokesperson for my party on external affairs, I want to make this very clear, as my colleague has done.
First of all, we have had a long-standing position of non-recognition of the annexation of the Baltic republics. That position remains. We fully support the importance of a dialogue, a constructive dialogue between the Baltic republics and the Soviet Union with respect to the facilitating of their desire to obtain sovereignty and self-determination.
Obviously this House and I join in condemning the violence that took place in Lithuania, the death of some 14 Lithuanians eight days ago, the violence and death in Latvia. Tragically, earlier today, we learned that there have been two explosions of undetermined origins in Estonia at a building in the Tallinn Shipyards and a centre for worker collectives. Fortunately there were no injuries, but we recall that similar explosions in Riga in early January preceded the recent events in Latvia.
I want to take this opportunity to indicate that we certainly, in general terms, support the position that the government has taken in response to this very difficult question. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has outlined that response. We welcome, particularly, his assurance that within the context of the United Nations this matter will be given high priority, whether it be in Geneva at the United Nations Human Rights Commission or at the Security Council. I would hope that we would be prepared, although not a member of the Security Council, to seek to have this matter raised there or in other fora including the CSCE.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs knows that I have communicated with him in respect of the question of observer status for the Baltic republics at CSCE meetings. I understand the consensus process at CSCE meetings, but I would hope that Canada would take a position now of support for observer status at the CSCE.
As well, my colleague referred to the fact that the eyes of the world have been so focused and so riveted on the situation in the gulf that not enough attention has been paid to the situation in the Baltic republics: in Lithuania, in Latvia, and hopefully not but possibly in Estonia.
I wanted to note as well that in the same context-and I will be brief-the eyes of the world have not been focused on another very serious violation of human rights. I am speaking here of the trials which are taking place in China of the Tiananmen Square dissidents. I have the same concern with respect to the lack of attention. Indeed a young Chinese citizen, Mao Jiye, Secretary-General of the Federation of Chinese Students and Scholars in Canada, attempted to visit China and was denied. I hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs will express his concern on this matter, as eloquently and as forcefully as he has done with respect to the Baltic republics.
In conclusion, I want to reinforce our full support for the measures that have been taken in this context and to urge that the United Nations, the community of nations, very forcefully make it clear to Mikhail Gorbachev, who has done so much over the past six years to give the world hope of a new beginning with glasnost and perestroika, will not abandon that very important course and will in fact ensure that the Baltic republics are no longer the scene of violence and death.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let

me begin by saying that I will be sharing my time on this side of the House with my colleagues.
I want to express appreciation to members of the House of Commons for agreeing to have this debate. Particularly I want to thank the Secretary of State for External Affairs for his excellent and thoughtful remarks tonight. The Secretary of State for External Affairs can be applauded for his commitment and indeed for his excellent work in the matters relating to the Baltic states.
Just one year ago, I had the opportunity, along with colleagues in this House of Commons, to visit Vilnius, Lithuania. At the invitation of Sajudis, the freedom movement in Lithuania, we witnessed the democratic election that gave an overwhelming victory to the principles of independence and self-government. The Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, after 50 years of domination by the Soviet Union, were set on a path for freedom and democracy.
To have been in Vilnius last year living with a Lithuanian family, speaking at meetings on behalf of freedom candidates, meeting students at the University of Vilnius, chatting with people in restaurants, stores and on the street, the determination and discipline of the people was clear. They wanted political and economic independence.
Upon returning to Canada, my colleagues and I set to work to establish the Canadian Parliamentary Group for the Baltic Peoples, a non-partisan group of MPs from all sides of the House, to work together with those Canadians with Baltic heritage or Baltic roots in order to advance in a concerted way our assistance, as well as to encourage our government's support and assistance for the realization of independence for Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia.
I want to thank the leaders of the Baltic community in Canada for their tremendous work. Particularly I want to mention Laas Levitt, President of the Estonian Central Council in Canada; Doctor Gurtis Silins, President of the Latvian National Federation in Canada; and A1 Pacecui-nis, Past President of the Lithuanian Canadian community. The work that they provide within the communities and the information support they give to parliamentarians are very much appreciated. All the members of the communities in the Baltic states are to be applauded for their good work.
The election in Lithuania was a one-issue election. It was independence, and it was an overwhelming victory. Now, just a few short months later with freedom and independence within reach, the oppressive Soviet regime, in spite of its words of glasnost, perestroika, openness and freedom, has hit these Baltic nations with the full force of the military.
The Soviets first responded to the calls of independence with an economic blockade of vital necessities. It was attempting to strangle the people into submission. When the blockade failed, the Soviets appeared to hold out the promise of negotiation. It is clear now that never was its intent. Now presidential rule has been threatened and the Soviet tanks have rolled in bringing back memories of previous atrocities.
Just this weekend, I heard the testimonial accounts of eyewitnesses from the three Baltic communities of the massacre, as well as the persecutions suffered by the men forced to conscript to an army not representative of their values, their beliefs or their ideals. I was moved to horror at the atrocities inflicted.
This issue is an international issue. It cannot rest untouched in the affairs of the Soviet Union. We have witnessed a side of Mikhail Gorbachev which is contrary to all the progress and reform made in that nation. We cannot ignore it. This is why it is so fundamentally important that we debate this crisis in the House of Commons tonight.
We stand resolute in support of the people of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia for their independence, to ensure freedom, democratic and human rights, and justice. Through the United Nations, the Human Rights Commission or the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, every possible effort must be made to set our position squarely on the agenda, that we accept nothing less than the independence of these nations.
I encourage parliamentary representation within our delegations. I urge our government to support the striking of a United Nations task force on the Baltic states to observe the events as they occur and report back to the international community.
I applaud the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I am pleased that Canada has suspended the earlier commitment to the Soviet Union to assist in its reforms.

Indeed, how could we continue to assist a country, the values of which obviously run contrary to our own. How could we provide assistance to a country, the president of which has gone back on his very assurances to our government that force would not be used in the Baltic states. I was also pleased to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs talk about the medical aid which would be sent directly to the Baltic states.
I want to speak about the information centre. The Secretary of State for External Affairs stated in his remarks that the establishment of an information centre was under review. I applaud that. I believe this to be an excellent initiative: to establish an information centre in order to make available all relevant information concerning events, as well as the safety of families in the Baltic states. I understand that a similar information centre has already been established in Stockholm.
I also urge our government to make every means available to those persons who wish to leave the Baltic states and come to Canada, especially those who are the victims of criminal acts and persecution.
Our parliamentary group has met with representatives of the Baltic communities in Canada. I am pleased to report to the House of Commons the appreciation extended to right hon. Prime Minister for his forthright and quick response by communicating with President Gorbachev, expressing the abhorrence of all Canadians of the unwarranted violence used against the people in the democratically elected Government of Lithuania.
In closing, we must continue as parliamentarians and as individuals committed to democracy to support the aspirations and the goals of the Baltic peoples in then-struggle and the realization of their independence.
