speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with an enormous sense of disappointment and foreboding for the future that I participate in this debate.
Over the past two or three years the relationship between the Soviet Union and the rest of the world has been characterized by one word: hope, hope of a new era in the history of the world.

Hope for independence and freedom, and with them a new meaning of reality not only in relations between nations but also in the spirit of the human soul.

Even as we have witnessed the difficulties and increasing dangers accompanying change in the Soviet Union, we have hoped that the leadership and the citizens of that vast land would find the will and the ways to continue their march toward the future. Today we must question that march and we must question its direction: to the future with confidence, or back to the past with fear and terror?
There can be no question of Canada's concern at events in the Baltic. We condemn, without reservation, the unwarranted and brutal violence with which democratically elected governments in Lithuania and Latvia and their institutions have been attacked.

We are not naive. We know and we understand the enormous pressure brought to bear on the Soviet Union president, but we also know-and we thought he knew- that there is no room for coercion and intimidation in the society he was defending and which was his aim, at least that is what we thought.

We still hope Mikhail Gorbachev stands for the free development and growth of democracy and for the self-determination which such democracy demands. We believe democracy offers to the Soviet Union, its peoples and its neighbours greater security and greater prosperity than they have witnessed under the old regime.
Where does the Soviet Union stand at this hour? Where is Mikhail Gorbachev? Where is glasnost at this hour of decision? Every one of us participating in this debate tonight knows full well the facts of history which brought the free and independent Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia under Stalin's rule 50-some years ago.
We know the brutal repression with which all opposition was eliminated. We know the enforced Russification with which the cultures of these peoples were suppressed. But we also know that that oppression failed.

We know here, in our own country, and in many others, how courageously and passionately the former citizens of these countries and their descendants kept alive their hopes and their dreams of free homelands through so many dark years.
With the changes President Gorbachev brought to the Soviet Union, we saw that the citizens living in those Baltic countries had kept alive those same hopes, those same dreams, no less brightly.
There are many things tanks and armoured vehicles can crush, but they cannot crush the idea of liberty once planted. That is the lesson of history we thought the new Soviet Union understood. The universal declaration of human rights, the Helsinki Accord, these, we thought and we had hoped, would be the pillars of any new relationship to form between constituent parts of this huge union. If they were to be called republics, we here in Canada looked for them to be republics in more than name only.

That is the evolution in which we have put our confidence and in which the Balkan states and their citizens have faith. When they were given the opportunity to cast their ballots, they did not hesitate. These are nascent democracies, as we can call them, but through their conviction and understanding they have shown wisdom and maturity beyond their years.

Are these brave hopes now to be ended in bloodshed and destruction? Is the Charter of Paris, signed only a few weeks ago, to become as worthless as so many other pieces of paper in history have become?
I know that all Canadians join me in urging President Gorbachev to stand with the believers in democracy and openness at this time and to demonstrate that courageous leadership for which he has been applauded by the whole world.
In the past year so many of the symbols of tyranny have been swept away, across Europe and in the Soviet Union itself. The walls have come down. The secret police organizations have been disbanded or recalled to barracks. The presses and broadcast towers of a free and uncensored media have begun to take their place.
The world has applauded this transformation and those who have made it possible. We have rejoiced that millions have found new purpose and new hope. What possible purpose can there be to end such progress?
Security? Can anyone seriously believe a return to the cold war can lead to greater security?
Prosperity? What prosperity is there in a new arms race, in the collapse of economic development that will follow new repression?
Tranquillity? Tranquillity in the streets of Vilnius and Riga will come with the sounds of citizens rejoicing in their freedom and in the things free citizens do, not in the sound of tanks and machine guns.
Canada has never recognized the annexation of the Baltic states by the Soviet Union and we will not. What we will recognize is whether the Soviet Union desires to continue or to withdraw from its new relationship with the world and with its own people.
We want for the Soviet Union every opportunity for peace, friendship and freedom and all that they can bring. But President Gorbachev must also know that Canadians will watch closely how he acts at this time.
We urge him to act with courage and with wisdom, for democracy, for freedom.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like all Canadians and like all freedom loving people around this world, I was absolutely shocked and disgusted by the events that have been taking place in Lithuania and more recently in Latvia in the last few days. It is even more shocking when one considers the fact that this is coming so hard on the heels of the events that have been taking place in the Persian Gulf.
I, like most members of this House, have a great many constituents and personal friends whose place of origin is the Baltic states. I have a Latvian Canadian Cultural Centre in my riding. I have a good many friends and constituents who are very close to that centre. The Estonia House is just on the border of my riding. Again, a good many constituents and friends are associated with Estonia House. Just a few short months ago, I had the opportunity of being at the Lithuanian Community House in Toronto to celebrate with some of the other members of this House the free and independent elec-

January 21, 1991
tions which had taken place in Lithuania for the first time since the end of the Second World War.
All members of this House and all Canadians are well aware of the very troubled existence that the Baltic states have had over the years. We are aware that they were independent in the 13th century. We are aware that they were dominated by their larger neighbours up until the end of the First World War. They became independent for a very brief period of time again between World War I and World War II and that independence was snuffed out by the Soviet Union in breach of non-aggression pacts signed with each of those three nations.
We are aware, as well, that the Baltic states were fought over by the Nazis and by the armies of the Soviet Union. Ultimately, they came to be dominated, after the Second World War as a result of the Yalta conference and the dividing up of spheres of influence throughout Europe, by the Soviet Union.
We know as well, however, that Canada has never recognized the illegal annexation or occupation of the Baltic states. We have always considered that legally they remain independent.
Now, just as they seemed about to gain their independence in fact as well as in law, that independence has been struck at again by the Soviet army. What can we do, and what should we do? We have heard that the Prime Minister has already condemned these actions. He has written to Mr. Gorbachev condemning these actions.
We know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has gone further, first of all, in indicating that we were reconsidering our aid to the Soviet Union and now, has indicated that we are suspending that aid. Many of my own constituents have pointed out other ways that we can act as well.
They suggested an emergency debate such as the one we are having tonight. They suggested that Canadian observers be sent to the Baltic states such as the Norwegians have sent. They suggested that we, again, insist that the U.S.S.R. stop the illegal and horrific actions that are taking place there. They suggested that UN Security Council can try to impose sanctions even though we know that the Soviet Union holds that veto power.
They have suggested UN observers, and they have suggested again that the UN impose sanctions. These are things that we might do unilaterally, but there are things that we should be doing through the United Nations as well, it seems to me, because we failed to bring about an effective and peaceful conclusion in the Persian Gulf.
What we must do now is try to find an effective and peaceful means of solving this problem with the Baltic states. At the same time, we must find it in a way which will guarantee once and for all the freedom, the democracy and the independence of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening I wish to describe the terrible conditions under which people in the Baltic countries are living. The situation in these republics is very serious. The attacks against these peoples will have dramatic consequences.
In this part of the world, where political foundations are so fragile, people are fighting for survival. The gulf war must not let us forget them. The tragic events of the last few days have shocked us all. They show us how vulnerable efforts to obtain more open and transparent government are. They also show that people cannot be repressed indefinitely. The desire for self-determination cannot be muffled forever. The history of the Baltic republics is written in blood. Devastated by war, abused by dictatorial regimes, the Baltic people have nevertheless survived. Perestroika had given these people hope. Unfortunately, interests with dictatorial tendencies want to snuff out this spark of freedom.
We now know there is no government that can extinguish the flame of the Baltic countries. The movement is irresistible. It points the way to a world where force will no longer be relevant.

The valiant efforts of the Baltic states have taught us much. They have taught us that moral principles, that principles of justice are the principles of nationhood.
Free elections were held in the Baltic states. In February, for instance, my colleague, the member for Parkdale-High Park, who is one of Canada's leading experts on eastern Europe, was a witness to the election in Lithuania. He told me, as he has said to this House

tonight, that those elections were fairly held. He has said that they observed the principles of democracy. He has said that their legislatures were democratically elected. Under these circumstances how can anybody now justify sending in troops to take away from the people of the Baltic countries their duly elected Parliament?
First Lithuania, then Latvia, how much longer before Estonia? The world must now speak with one unequivocal voice. What must the world do? First, it must recognize that the simple niceties of diplomatic language will not deter those who would take away a people's freedom by force. It must recognize that vague protests and economic aid possibly withheld are simply not enough. What must the world do?
First, it must put real weight into the economic levers that the world has at its disposal. To that end, I would congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the announcement that he made tonight.
Second, the world must introduce a resolution in the United Nations Security Council condemning Soviet aggression. The motion may well be defeated but the point must be made. It will not go unnoticed.
There are other measures that we must take as well. In Canada, we must pay more than lip service to the very real fact, which is the absolute independence of the Baltic states. We must say that de jure recognition is no longer sufficient, that the Baltic states are entitled to real recognition. A people who have held free elections, a people who have fought for their independence, are entitled to full diplomatic accreditation.
Again I refer to the question of my colleague from Parkdale-High Park when he asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs why he did not meet the leaders of the Baltic states, not in his simple capacity as a parliamentarian, but in his full capacity as the representative of this country, the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
There are other things. We must call a special meeting of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe to condemn the very real menace that the threat to the Baltic states poses to the peace of Europe and the world.
Finally, because my time is limited, Mr. Speaker, we must accept as refugees those from the Baltic countries who find their way here. That the government of the Soviet Union is considering deporting young men whose only crime is that they refuse to report to an army whose ultimate purpose may well be to shoot their own people is simply unthinkable.
Freedom is not the cause of destabilization. What are the objections to doing that which is right? Well, there are those who say that we must not destabilize Mikhail Gorbachev. There are those who say we must not destabilize the Soviet Union. I would argue the opposite.
The world owes a great deal to Mikhail Gorbachev, but he is now in a battle with conservative forces who would undo him and would undo everything that he has done. Those forces must understand that the free world will not stand for any backsliding. They must be told that Mikhail Gorbachev was right to begin with, and that he is wrong now. We must make it clear to the Soviet president that we will stand behind those who speak for freedom. Destabilization in the U.S.S.R. will not come from giving freedom to the Baltic states, it will come from refusing that freedom.
The Baltic states represent no threat. The threat comes, as it did indeed on the weekend, from the 300,000 people who demonstrated in Moscow, from the countless thousands who demonstrated throughout the Soviet Union against the great brutality that was demonstrated in Vilnius and in Riga. The Russian people, too, want their freedom. They know that it is linked to freedom elsewhere.
In conclusion, the Soviet Union is in the grip of terrible economic chaos. Its leadership must understand that economic progress without political freedom is simply impossible. The Soviet Union must understand that we are on the threshold of a new world order and that the Baltic states are a symbol of that order.
The Soviet Union must understand that all our fates, all around the world and indeed in this Chamber, are tied to the battle that three small but very, very courageous countries are waging.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my limited time, I would first like to compliment my colleague, the hon. member for La-Salle-Emard, who has been working closely with my colleague, the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park, in organizing, with all members of this House today, an emergency debate on this issue.
I want to read into the record a letter I received from a gentleman representing members of the business community, Mr. Peteris Kusmanis, from my riding. I think he summarized the situation well. He writes:
As a member of the Business Community, I am concerned with what is happening in the Soviet Union, particularly with the use of force to crush the democratically elected governments of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia. We cannot have mutually beneficial economic relations with the Soviet Union until the Soviet Union demonstrates that it is truly committed to democracy and free enterprise, and that it is worthy of our trust. The Soviet Union was apparently headed in the right direction-perestroika, glasnost, democratic elections-but the events of the last months have proven that perestroika and glasnost are a farce. I appeal to you to support or introduce a call for an all-party resolution today to condemn the Soviet attack yesterday on the democratically elected government of Latvia. The House of Commons should hold an IMMEDIATE emergency debate on the Baltic situation. Sanctions must be taken against the U.S.S.R. Canada must urge its partners in NATO, the CSCE and the United Nations to do the same; the U.S. is key in this matter and Brian Mulroney should be on the phone to George Bush to urge the U.S. to take strong action immediately.
Until freedom is restored to the Baltic States, and until the Soviet Union proves that it is committed to a free market system, there should be no thought of economic aid to the Soviet Union. This situation demands immediate action -
Many of my constituents are reflecting Mr. Kusmanis' point of view and I want to go back to the hon. member from Edmonton and his thoughts when he talked about being in the Soviet Union last year right around this time. I, too, was there speaking at an environmental conference where there was so much hope and so much feeling that we were all heading in the right direction.
Here we are tonight in this emergency debate, frustrated, hopes shattered. It is only by all members of the House uniting and sending a strong message to the Soviet Union that we can keep a flicker of hope that maybe some action will be taken. We hope Mr. Gorbachev will take a stand and for starters crush the action
that is going on in the Baltic States so that we might regain the hope that we had a year ago that he was going in the right direction.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the past 18 months the world, especially the western world, has witnessed a rollercoaster of hopes and expectations. It was 18 months ago when we began hearing the faint stirrings, the evergrowing stirrings, of hope for freedom in those countries which we used to call the east bloc countries in the days of the Iron Curtain.
We witnessed events almost beyond belief in the ensuing weeks which culminated in the tearing down of the Berlin wall.
It was not peace that was breaking out. These nations had experienced 40 years of a kind of peace all over eastern Europe. It is not the kind of peace we cherish, but it was a kind of peace, and it was not peace that was breaking out, it was freedom that broke out at that time.
But the forerunner to that experience was a statement by the Soviet Union, an admission on the part of the Soviet Union that the Molotov-von Ribbentrop agreement of 1939-1940 was in fact an illegal transaction.
This is what three'generations of Estonians, Latvians, and Lithuanians had been waiting for. Those people had been raped and pillaged by two European countries under an illegal agreement. Now a confession from the Soviet Union declared that to be illegal.
Therefore, it is now incumbent on the Soviet Union, since it has admitted its guilt, to undo the wrong of that treaty. That is what the debate is about tonight. Peace has been there, but now freedom is breaking out as witnessed, as several of our colleagues have spoken tonight, in the elections of the past year. Freedom is breaking out, but this presents President Gorbachev with an enormous problem.
In the ensuing 40 years, those countries have experienced interlocking populations, interlocking cultures, ideologies, goals, economies, all interwoven. How do you unscramble that egg? That is the difficulty facing President Gorbachev. When 50 per cent of the population of one of those countries are actually Russians, or citizens of the Soviet Union, that is a problem. It needs to be
January 21, 1991

solved. We should not retreat from it, but we must acknowledge that that problem exists.
We should also acknowledge that the problems will not become smaller. They will become greater as the years go by as long as that is ignored by the Soviet Union.
It is important to remember that these people have now tasted and experienced freedom as they never had known it before. They will not be satisfied until it is theirs permanently. They will not be denied. Suppression of that hunger for freedom will simply lead to greater explosions in the future.
It is important to notice that the Baltic people are trying to do it right. They are not trying to thumb their noses at the Soviet Union. They are trying to do it peacefully and by negotiations, and they are acting in good faith. Up to this point, they have not been rewarded for their good faith and for trying to do it right.
Canada has several responsibilities. First, we must sound the alarm that something is going drastically wrong in those countries. We must sound the alarm to the world. We cannot sit by, simply clucking our tongues and pretending it will go away.
We must learn from the mistake that we have experienced in the Middle East. Witness the eight-year war between Iraq and Iran when one million people were killed. The world stood by and said: "Isn't that terrible?" When Saddam Hussein was willing to sacrifice 50,000 lives just to capture one town, we stood by and we clucked our tongues as he gassed his own citizens, the Kurds. We did not say very much. Then, he moved into Kuwait, and we realized we had to do something and do it now. We need to learn from the experience of the Middle East that we cannot allow a repetition of that kind of pattern in the Baltic states.
Just four weeks ago, I met with a young man from my constituency. He is a professor of international economics and finance at UBC on leave studying in Finland the events of the Baltic states. He told me then, just before New Years that what the leaders in the Baltic states feared the most was that the heightening of the activity in the Middle East was going to give an opportunity to the conservative reactionary forces of the Soviet Union to move into the Baltic states. While everybody was
distracted in the Middle East, it could move into the Baltic states. Their prophesies have become true and we must sound the alarm.
The second thing we must do is stand by the Baltic people. We must let them know that we encourage them, that we stand with them, that we cherish their freedom with them, and that we want them to experience it the way we experience it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
We must let them know that we are not simply mouthing words, but we want them to cherish our freedoms. Therefore, we welcome the announcement by the secretary of state tonight that he has already suspended some of the present negotiations and initiatives that have taken place between Canada and the Soviet Union. They have been suspended.
Second, he is now initiating new ways of working with the Baltic people. We must meet with them. We must spend time with them. We must walk along side of them. We must take these new initiatives, some of which the secretary of state has announced tonight.
We must sound the alarm and we must encourage. We cannot allow the mistakes of the Middle East to be repeated in the Baltic states.
I welcome the debate tonight, and the only point I would make regarding my friend, the hon. member for LaSalle-Emard, is this. He said that it is worth the risk, destabilizing the Soviet Union and maybe allowing President Gorbachev to be set aside. It sounds very attractive if Mr. Gorbachev does not bring the reforms necessary-

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the Canadian House of Commons tonight to join with colleagues on all sides of this House to condemn and to

lament the armed suppression of the peoples in the Baltic republics and the curtailment of their freedoms.
Just recently I was browsing through one of the recent biographies about Mikhail Gorbachev. There were grouped on some pages a series of photographs. One seemed almost inexplicable. It was a full-page photograph of President Gorbachev by himself in a park, crouched down, feeding a squirrel. What was written underneath that was the statement: "The tragedy of Mikhail Gorbachev is that he will be unable to finish his own revolution". Why that picture, why that prophecy is hard to say, but certainly what we are seeing here is something that we often see with revolutionary change, that there is a period of retrenchment.
Just as George Bernard Shaw taught us that paradoxes are the only truths, we see a profound paradox in this situation, for the Gorbachev revolution as epitomized by perestroika and glasnost was accompanied also by a clear movement toward democracy and a clear suppression of the old instinct of totalitarian states to call out the army at the moment of crisis.
It was not the first time in the past few years that in the countries such as Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary we saw efforts to overthrow the regime that had been imposed since 1945. It had happened in 1956 in Budapest for Hungary. It had happened in 1968 in Prague for Czechoslovakia.
The difference this time was that the Red Army remained in the barracks and it remained there because Mikhail Gorbachev instructed that it should be so. So the paradox that we face tonight is that it is under this same regime, the same leader, that in fact military suppression has become the sad signature in already two of the Baltic republics, Lithuania and now Latvia.
At issue now is the future make-up of the Soviet Union. Mr. Gorbachev, it appears, is bent on maintaining control of a slightly decentralized federation of Soviet republics. The democratization that he once promoted stops short it seems of democratic self-determination for individual republics.
The Baltic peoples, on the other hand, took the Soviet leader's ideas seriously, drawing from glasnost and perestroika the logical conclusions that all republics would be free to administer their own political and economic programs. The differences have now become very clear.
While Mikhail Gorbachev preaches reform, the Baltic peoples practise it.
Tonight at six o'clock, I met with the Vice-President of Latvia, here in the East Block, in the company of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. What impressed me most particularly about his many messages to us was his statement that the people of Latvia have been making a journey in the past months, and they do not now want to go back. There is a palpable feeling of new power of democratic realization in many of the republics, including Ukraine which I visited last October, Kazakhstan, and elsewhere, Georgia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and the Russian republic itself. So, now is a time when we must not send the wrong signal.
Two years ago on March 4 when I addressed the annual congress of the Baltic veterans in Canada, I quoted from books where on earlier occasions the freedom fighters in those republics had prepared to seek to overthrow the existing authorities and re-establish a free and democratic society. They had based part of their initiative on statements made by leaders in the west and their assumption that those words would be translated into material support at the time of their uprising. Tragically, that support was not there when they moved and when they expected it.
Now we come to the need, as many members have said, to match our words with actions. That is why I fully endorse and gladly support everything that was contained in the outstanding speech this evening here in the House by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I am sure he and members of the government did not come lightly to announcing to us tonight the suspension of the $150 million line of credit and all the other initiatives that he referred to that are now in a state of suspension. The member from Winnipeg also referred to the sense of hope that we had seen in all of these recent developments, so tonight is not a happy night when we see the necessity of taking these steps.
We cannot have this debate in the House and be unmindful that our country is again at war in the Persian Gulf. For the fifth time in this century our country is at war and we are once again, as Canadian poet Robert W. Service said, staring into the aching womb of night. There is nothing about this war that we relish or

welcome. We are there because of a commitment and support of the United Nations.
We are considering tonight the situation of Latvia and Lithuania, countries that also were invaded, occupied and annexed by a neighbouring power. So we have many parallels here which cannot be lost on any of us tonight who are grappling with the difficult legal dilemma that the Soviet Union, as a member of the United Nations, considers to be an internal matter and not something subject to the purview of the United Nations.
In conclusion, I want to say that last October when I was in the Soviet Union, I saw many things that would encourage all of us, the kinds of changes for which we called for years and years now actually happening. I also saw a country that in so many respects was simply one level above chaos. So many people were determined to throw over the old order, a system that for 70 years had preached success but had produced shortages, failure, repression and extermination of millions of freedom loving people.
As I left, the only question in my mind as I felt that palpable sense of freedom, that rising surge of reform and democracy was the question of who controls the Red Army, because as Lenin had once said, the communist party is the glue that holds the Soviet Union together. The communist party today has atrophied and withered away and is no longer any such glue. We are, I am afraid, seeing that in these last remnant hours of this 20th century's last empire, the only force that is available is the force of arms. Let us all hope that the measures taken here and the voices expressed here can in time, and I mean now, cause this to be reversed.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
In his wisdom, the Speaker of the House has permitted this important emergency debate to take place and on behalf of the Canadians of Baltic origins in my riding of Hamilton West, I thank you, Sir. I thank my colleague, the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park for his tireless effort as co-chair of the Canadian Parliamentary Group for the Baltic Peoples, that all-party, all-member group of which I am so proud to be a member.
Members of the Society of East Central European Nations at Hamilton, Ontario, remember all too well
what Gromyko said when he was succeeded by Gorbachev. He said: "Behind his nice smile he has iron teeth". It is a cruel quote to be restated here tonight, especially in light of all the good that Gorbachev has presided over as of late. It is a cruel statement maybe, but not for the Lithuanians, not for the Latvians and hopefully not for the Estonians.
Just yesterday in downtown Hamilton, which was the first municipality in the country to draw up a resolution in support of democracy for Lithuania, appealing to the federal government to take a strong position in support of Lithuania, it was a bitter wind that swirled around the hundreds of protesters who gathered outside Hamilton City Hall, the members of the Lithuanian, Latvian, Estonian and Ukrainian communities who agreed that the struggle in the Baltic states is no less serious a threat to world peace than the war in the Persian Gulf and that if it is forgotten, we will all pay a heavy price.
Showing their support for the Baltic states, some demonstrators carried their national flag. Others waved placards which read: "Peace not bloodshed". Another said: "Gorbachev, Nobel Peace Prize Winner", except the word "peace" was scratched out and the word "war" was inserted so the sign read: "Gorbachev Nobel War Prize Winner". Still another picket sign read: "Talks not tanks". A very touching moment was when a group of school-aged children took their black bows as symbols and placed them on a symbolic tree, an evergreen tree.
Yes, I and many members of this House feel again the fear and the frustrations of those valiant people whose homelands face the bonds of tyranny. Tension in the Baltics is high. In fact, there is growing fear that the unwarranted military crackdown used against the people and democratically elected government in Lithuania, which killed 13 people, injured 165, and 65 people are missing and the attack by Soviet troops on a Latvian police headquarters resulting in the deaths of five, will soon spread to Estonia because there in Estonia concrete barriers have been erected around the Parliament Buildings where the people wait and watch hour to hour.
My fear is that the world attention and much of the resources of the news media have been diverted from the troop movements and bloodshed in the Baltics to the Persian Gulf war. If allowed to continue, Gorbachev may

succeed through the back door that which he could not possibly accomplish walking in through the front door.
Many words have been written by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He strongly protests, in fact condemns, the brutal and unacceptable Soviet crackdowns in Lithuania and Latvia. Many words have been spoken in protests and demonstrations in my riding of Hamilton West, in the riding of Parkdale-High Park and other ridings of this House, and in demonstrations around the world. Many words will be spoken in this emergency debate tonight.
However, it is concrete action which I urge the government to implement continually in order to impress upon the Soviet Union the urgency of this grave situation. "What action", one may ask. We promote constructive dialogue between the Soviet Union and the Baltic states, the aim of which is the peaceful resolution of the crisis. In the words of one of my constituents-and I will use only her initials to respect her privacy-E.G. on Emerson Street, writes:
As you are no doubt aware, the Baltic countries lost their independence when the Soviet army illegally occupied them in 1940. Although Canada steadily maintains a policy of non-recognition de jure of this occupation, for which I and my fellow exiles are grateful, in actual fact Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania with their western European outlook and work ethic continue to function as colonies of the Soviet empire.
Recent political activities of the popular fronts in these countries and their supporters have forcefully shown the world their abiding desire for the restoration of freedom and dignity in their lives.
They need Canada's help.
Can Canada help? I congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs for meeting with the Soviet ambassador today and for the announcements that he has made here tonight. Canada can play a vital role by hearing the desires of the Baltic Canadian communities.
The Lithuanian Canadian community asks the Canadian government to take the following actions in the wake of the brutal crackdown in Vilnius by the Soviet army:
First, to impose sanctions on the U.S.S.R. until it withdraws its tanks and paratroopers from Vilnius and enters into negotiations with the legitimate government of Lithuania.
Second, to accord diplomatic recognition immediately to the democratically elected Government of the Republic of Lithuania, led by President Landsbergis.
Third, to introduce a Canadian resolution in the United Nations condemning the Soviet aggression to push for an emergency debate of the UN Security Council in order to debate the Baltic crisis.
Fourth, to call a special meeting of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe to condemn the assault on Lithuania as a threat to the peace of Europe.
Then we hear from the Latvian community which says clearly that this warning had no effect on Soviets. The Canadian Latvian community is outraged by the senseless tragedy of Soviet black berets killing and maiming innocent civilians and journalists in Riga. It calls on the Canadian government to cease all assistance to the Soviet Union immediately; to impose trade and economic sanctions, which we are glad to hear have begun tonight; to call an emergency debate in the House of Commons, in which we are participating here tonight; to call on the United Nations to send observers to the Baltic states; and to continue to raise the Baltic issue at the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe by stressing that Soviet actions will continue to threaten the peace of Europe until democracy is restored.
My Baltic constituents say they look forward to learning that members of Parliament, privileged to serve, have helped the Baltic nations in their struggle for the restoration of their economic and cultural sovereignty.
On their behalf, I implore the Secretary of State for External Affairs to use every practical, peaceful tool at his disposal, such as the one he announced here tonight, to pressure the Soviet Union into negotiating the terms of independence which we pray will resolve the legitimate concerns of the Baltic states.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate this evening on the situation in the Baltic states.

It is very difficult when the focus of attention in the world is on another part of the world, on the Persian Gulf, to draw the attention of many people to the
January 21, 1991

concerns that many of us have for the people of the Baltic republics: Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia.
However, it is of great importance for the world community, as an international community, to draw its attention to each and every sector of the world where concerns such as those we have all been expressing tonight need to be brought to bear. It is particularly important when so many in this country and elsewhere question the actions of the international community in the Persian Gulf, because they perceive there to be a double standard at practice in the world.
If the world community, through gaining experience in co-operative action and collective security, is to achieve a lasting world peace on the basis of those principles, it will be necessary to establish a standard that can be applied in many situations, not just in those where specific and important economic interests prevail.
All of us feel a very great disappointment at what has transpired in the Soviet Union and in the Baltic states, very great disappointment made that much greater by the amount of hope we all felt for this regime led by a new man, a man who looked affable, competent and, as Margaret Thatcher once said, "like a man with whom we could do business". Now, having awarded him the Nobel Peace Prize, we find that in his nation troops are firing guns and driving tanks over people who are speaking on behalf of democratic reforms in their own country.
It is important for Canadians to remember that the history of the Baltic republics is one which in this century has included the subjugation by the Soviet Union as a result of the pact between Nazi Germany and Stalin which led to their being acquired in 1940. To this day, Canada has not recognized that subjugation of the Baltic states.
We still had so much hope. Of course, they did not immediately permit their independence, but when we think back over the years of the cold war we think of what happened in Hungary in 1956 and in Czechoslovakia in 1968, the building of the Berlin wall in 1961, the enormous change that occurred, and the years and years of arms reduction talks which went on and on and seemed to go nowhere.
Suddenly, with this new leader in the Kremlin, the world seemed to take on a different face. Freedom seemed to spring up in the Soviet Union: the right of dissent, with people marching in the streets protesting
what their government was saying; Soviet politicians and journalists coming to Canada and telling us what was happening; and the freedom of expression, the freedom of opinion, in the journals of the Soviet Union. Suddenly the door seems to be slamming shut. Of course we are disappointed.
This is important, in light of some of the comments that President Gorbachev made. This is not a question of law and order in Lithuania, in particular. This is not a question of law and order. This is a question of military force being applied against the democratically elected government of the state of Lithuania. Those elections were not held by some outside power. They were authorized and legitimized, even by the government of the Soviet Union. They were held under international supervision in Lithuania, the result of which was to elect the government that last March 11 voted, not by a narrow majority but unanimously, to declare the independence of Lithuania from the Soviet Union.
What an exciting event that was. I have a report from the Washington Post dated March 12, 1990, indicating the excitement felt by the people who witnessed that occasion. Tears streamed down their faces as they realized that their country again had the prospect of becoming independent. Then a few months later, 10 months later, that hope seems to be dying in the face of Soviet tanks.
There should be no questions where Canada stands on this issue. Canada has never recognized the occupation of the Baltic republics by the Soviet Union. That position has remained consistent, no matter what party has been in government.
I would like to read from a letter dated April 29, 1983 from the then Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Hon. Allan J. MacEachen, who wrote at that time:
Canada does not recognize de jure the incorporation of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania into the Soviet Union. The Soviet Government is well aware of our position which has been firmly maintained over the last forty years. In following this policy the Canadian Government expresses its continuing disapproval of the forcible incorporation of the Baltic states.
In the face of that statement-and I have no reason to believe the current government has changed its position on it-I fail to understand why the Secretary of State for External Affairs must meet with Lithuanian and Latvian representatives in his parliamentary capacity and not in

January 21, 1991
his ministerial capacity. He should be ashamed to refuse to do that.
It is important for the Soviet Union to understand that the national ideal in the Baltic republics is integrated with the democratic ideals. Mr. Gorbachev must be brought to understand by representations-and I understand that they have been clear and strong from our government-from our government and other western governments indicating that the concept of democratic reform incorporates into it the right to self-determination of peoples, particularly in republics such as the Baltics where national ideals are long held and national traditions clearly exist.
Just as it is impossible to stop the wind, leaders of countries throughout the world must understand it is impossible to stop the winds of freedom which are blowing. We felt their sensation in China. We have seen them blow down the Berlin wall. We have seen them blow away governments in eastern Europe. We feel their gentle breezes in other parts of the world. The winds of freedom and democracy are blowing in the Soviet Union.
The choice is clear. That government can either harness the wind or it can attempt to resist it. The benefits of harnessing the wind are a people, proud of their land and able to dedicate themselves to making it better, to building a strong economy, to building a land based on compassion and the principles of democracy. To resist is to build anger and frustration, to build sadness and despair, and to ensure that economic reforms will not succeed. I think the choice is an obvious one.
I applaud our government for the actions that the minister has announced tonight. I would hope that actions such as those and others duplicating them around the world will assist Mr. Gorbachev in making his case in his country that he can either succeed in his negotiations with the west, build the new world order and a stronger, healthier Soviet economy, or he can go back to the old ways, face the enormous resistance that western countries will bring to bear on him and find that nothing will dig his country out of the economic pit into which it has fallen.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me five minutes and thanks also to
the "bloc conservateur" for giving me five minutes of their speaking time. As a member of the Bloc quebecois, I also wish to condemn the Soviet Union's actions against democracy and the Baltic peoples. Quebecers understand what it must feel like because they had the same experience in 1970. They too saw Canadian tanks roll in to repress a growing democracy. If we compare what is happening in Lithuania and in other countries throughout the world with what happened in Quebec during the October Crisis, we see many similarities. We remember that Canadian tanks entered Quebec and that the Canadian government suspended the rights of individuals as is happening today in Lithuania. They sent soldiers and tanks, like today in Lithuania. They arrested people without cause. More than 400 Quebecers were detained in prison, although they had no connection whatsoever with the October Crisis and had not been in involved in anti-social or other activities. These people were kept in prison and denied the right to call a lawyer. They were tortured. They were threatened as people are being threatened today in Lithuania, in the Baltic States. After those arrests, people lost their jobs forever and their reputations were smeared forever as well.
Mr. Speaker, no country in the world is immune from such abuse, such attacks on democracy. We must not turn a blind eye to our own actions that were also attacks on democracy.
Not long ago, Mr. Speaker, in 1989, China used tanks to subjugate democracy, and the House of Commons condemned that decision. In 1990, the House of Commons condemned the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq. In 1991, it condemns the invasion of Lithuania by Soviet tanks. But I may remind the House that in 1970, it remained silent when Canadian tanks entered Quebec to subjugate democracy.
However, after listening to speeches by hon. members this evening, I found their resolve to defend all parts of the world that are seeking democracy and sovereignty very reassuring. I am therefore very confident that in the future, Quebec will be a democratic and sovereign country and that members of this House will rise to defend it with as much zeal as they did this evening in defending Lithuania.
January 21, 1991

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to be part of this debate. I am really saddened by the developments. We have seen profound and regrettable acts by the U.S.S.R. against the Baltic states.
I have had the opportunity to visit the Soviet Union on three occasions, the most recent last June. There really were some signs of progress, progress in moving down the road towards democracy. But one only had to be there a few hours to know how fragile that progress was. Perhaps the many people in the Soviet Union and the Baltic states might have had their expectations too high because that road to democracy is going to take quite some time.
I want to commend the patience and the resolve of the people in the Baltic states. I want to commend the patience, as well, of the Canadians whose origins are Lithuanian, Latvian and Estonian. This year they will be organizing the 19th Baltic dinner, which they organized on the Hill to speak to parliamentarians and leaders about their important cause.
I would like to recount some of the statements, commitments and actions of the last two weeks. On January 8, this statement came from the Secretary of State for External Affairs:
- Joe Clark, today expressed concern about the announced movement of military forces into the Baltic states, Ukraine and several other republics of the Soviet Union.
"Our concerns have been forcefully conveyed today to the Soviet Ambassador," stated Mr. Clark. "We are urging restraint on all sides in this potentially dangerous situation".
Mr. Clark called on Soviet authorities to refrain from further intimidation and the use of force, expressing the hope that solutions to the outstanding differences between the republics and Moscow can be negotiated.
Mr. Clark recalled that Soviet Foreign Minister Shevardnadze had assured him several times that there would be no crackdown in the Baltic States, and that President Gorbachev had reaffirmed this to Prime Minister Mulroney.
On January 9, a letter was sent from the Canadian Parliamentary Group for the Baltic Peoples, signed by the chair, the hon. member for Scarborough Centre and
the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park and, of course, the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona was involved in this. It was sent to the Soviet ambassador in Canada, Mr. Richard Ovinnikov, and it states:
On behalf of the Canadian Parliamentary Group for the Baltic Peoples, we wish to register our strong protest at the recent movement of Soviet troops into the Baltic states.
This action is totally unacceptable and is contrary to previous statements made by your government. It was our expectation that negotiations would proceed in order to resolve the differences which exist between your government and the Baltic States.
Two days later, on January 11, this press release was issued, on behalf of Mr. Clark, and it stated, in part:
"We deplore the use of force against the democratically elected government and the people of Lithuania," Mr. Clark stated. "Such actions are contrary to the assurances given to me by Foreign Minister Shevardnadze and repeated to Prime Minister Mulroney by President Gorbachev, that there would be no crackdown in the Baltics."
Mr. Clark urged restraint in this dangerous situation and called on the Soviet authorities to refrain from further violence. He emphasized that the Soviet Union must adhere to its obligations under the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe (CSCE) and negotiate solutions based on the principles of the Helsinki Final Act.
Two days after that, January 13, a news release from the Prime Minister's office included these remarks:
The Prime Minister deeply regrets that these actions have taken place, contrary to explicit assurances given to Canada by Mr. Gorbachev. The Prime Minister stressed the need for Mr. Gorbachev to quickly and unequivocally condemn such behaviour.
The Prime Minister appealed for Mr. Gorbachev to show restraint and avoid further bloodshed. He urged the Soviet President to seek solutions consistent with the Helsinki Final Act, the Charter of Paris and the legitimate aspirations of Lithuania and the other Baltic states. Democracy cannot exist without respect for fundamental human rights and freedoms.
The Prime Minister advised that Canada was reviewing its offer of technical assistance and new lines of credit for the purchase of foodstuffs.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs said tonight that program has been suspended.
On January 15, two days after that, the special motion which was agreed to by all members was put to the House, and it reads:
Be it resolved
That this House condemns the brutal and unacceptable Soviet crackdown in Lithuania, and calls upon President Gorbachev and the U.S.S.R. authorities to refrain from using further violence against the people and democratically elected governments of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia.

S. ft 52
On top of all that, just last evening we saw on television and heard the news that the Soviet Black Berets attacked and assaulted a building in Riga, Latvia. It is reported that four people were killed and at least 10 were injured. This is another regrettable backward step, a sad step, that is repugnant in the eyes of most people.
Canadians with roots in the Baltic countries are very concerned. They have been worried and frustrated for years but they had their hopes picked up in the last year or two. Now they have been dashed again by these developments.
I received a letter from Mr. and Mrs. A. P. Stanenas in Thornhill and I would like to read a bit of that, Mr. Speaker. It is addressed to me and it says:
In view of the ongoing Soviet atrocities against the people and the
government of Lithuania we urge you -
(2) That you urge the Prime Minister of Canada to call for a meeting of the United Nations Security Council and to sponsor a resolution condemning the use of acts of bloodied aggression against the people of Lithuania and ordering the withdrawal of Soviet military forces out of the Republic of Lithuania.
Also, a few hours ago Mr. Voldemars Berkis, a Canadian from Latvia telephoned me very concerned and worried. He had several questions and I will just state two or three. Basically what he wanted to know was why the double standard, why do some infractions, why do some human rights violations seem to be dealt with more quickly than the problems in the Baltic states. Why not have this debated at the United Nations was another question.
He had many other concerns about the decades of talk without concrete action. What do you say to a man like that, Mr. Speaker, other than that all members on all sides of this House will tiy to stand together this time and really move toward concrete action.
Earlier today I asked the right hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs a question in the House. The gist of it was that the third round of the CSCE, which is emphasizing the human dimension, is being held in Moscow later this summer. The U.S.S.R. is hosting it so I asked the minister if we would give some thought to reconsidering being a participant and if some of these violations are not dealt with very quickly maybe we
should withdraw from that conference. It sounds harsh but it is time for harsh action on behalf of the people of the Baltic states.
In closing, I want to assure all Canadians of Baltic origin that all members of this House are going to do every practical thing possible in the coming weeks and months to help them achieve that dream of theirs, that dream of independence, that dream of freedom, that somehow it will be reached and these atrocities and setbacks that have happened far too many times will be history.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have this opportunity to speak on this topic tonight, the special debate on the Baltic issue.
I want to thank the members of this House who have been so active in keeping this issue alive and being a driving force to make this debate happen tonight, the members for Scarborough Centre, Parkdale-High Park, and Winnipeg Transcona. Without their driving energy, quite possibly this debate would not have come tonight, even though I know all of us in this House have received phone calls from all over Canada asking that this House come together to consider this most important issue.
I want to thank the people in my riding of London- Middlesex whose origin and family ties are back to the Baltics. This community of several hundred families in London and southwestern Ontario has done a great deal to enrich the culture and the life of our community. It has been a great addition for all of us. The knowledge they have passed on to their fellow Canadians about their roots and their part of the world has helped all of us to a better understanding.
The lesson that we have learned from these people is one that I guess is not a big surprise to most Canadians, that these three countries were independent countries. They had self-determination.
Self-determination is really the point of my speech tonight, because clearly self-determination is on everyone's mind at the present time in the Persian Gulf, whether one is a Kuwaiti, a Palestinian, an Arab of another descent, or a Canadian who is fighting for the freedom of self-determination of those countries. We are all very interested in self-determination and, as
January 21, 1991

parliamentarians, this is the thing that we are pushing for the most.
The U.S.S.R.'s persistence in keeping self-determination from these three countries came as quite a surprise to us. Even though Gorbachev opened up the Soviet, and opened up this part of the world so that it looked like self-determination was possible with free elections for the first time, which some of my colleagues had the good fortune of witnessing, we are now finding out that in fact his intentions were not real. In the last few days, with brutal reality, the Black Berets have moved in and trampled the rights and trampled the growth of self-determination. These people and Canadians are indignant, and rightly so, to this action.
We have heard tonight from the Secretary of State for External Affairs that Canada has taken, through the actions of our Prime Minister and through his own department, some very dramatic and hopefully helpful gestures. One is freezing the $150 million help to the Soviet Union effective today, which I think was a very good move. But more than this is in order. As a group of parliamentarians committed to self-determination and to the rights of the Baltic people, we have to go further than this.
There has been talk tonight about acting on the recommendations all of us receive from our communities. I have met with the Baltic communities in London and London-Middlesex and found that their concerns were echoed here tonight in the House.
I hope that actions will be taken in the United Nations at the Security Council. We look forward to that. We have already talked about the government's action, which I hope will be a help.
Tonight, I see some of my colleagues in the House who are members of the executive of the Canada-Europe Parliamentary Association. That group has representation of all the parties in the House. Under the aegis of yourself, Sir, I think it can provide a veiy useful service to the newly elected governments of the three countries, as we have done with fledgling governments in Hungary, Czechoslovakia, and Poland.
The association has been veiy active and would like to be active in the Baltic countries in terms of helping them with their role as parliamentarians and helping them, through the eyes of other countries, to see their legitimate practice as they work towards maintaining their
right of self-determination. Also, to put the backbone on that, these countries, these governments, and these parliamentarians need help in developing an economic infrastructure.
The Canada-Europe Parliamentary Association has worked very hard indeed with the parliaments of the other eastern European countries. In fact, over a period of a year, it has had some very significant results in terms of helping with their economic strengths.
As the economic strengths come together, so does the rigor of the people. When some citizens take it upon themselves to usurp the control of the government, as clearly is the case in Lithuania and certainly yesterday and today in Riga, where some members are saying that they see the elected government as being out of step with the realities of that particular country. Its goals are in effect going back to the U.S.S.R., using the Black Berets to come in and trample the rights of the elected governments which are in fact carrying almost the self-determination of the people of those states.
Clearly, they need to be strengthened as parliamentarians. They need all the help they can get from equivalent countries around the world and this Parliament. I think I can speak for all members in the House that we will definitely commit ourselves to this endeavour. Through the Canada-Europe Parliamentary Association, we want the communities in Canada from the three Baltic countries to know that all members are committed to working with the newly elected governments in those three countries.
We will find ways to work together so this base of parliamentarians which, as I said at the opening of my remarks, began with three of our colleagues who have taken this case up and have worked with Baltic Canadians in a very positive way to bring the issue in front of all Canadians. Thus all 26 million know now that it is not just in the Persian Gulf where self-determination is at risk, but, in fact, it is in northeast Europe where three countries, whom Canada has always recognized with the right to self determination, are very much finding their rights lost.
We want those people in Canada, as well in those three countries to know that this Parliament is strongly behind them. There is one association under your direction, Sir, which is going to make every effort to speed up this process and to help them through the

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has already been said by others, it is indeed an honour to rise tonight to speak to this emergency resolution. This motion has come about as a result of the events that have taken place over the last number of days in the Baltic states and the increase in military activity in all of these areas. I feel strongly tonight that Canada's relationship with the Soviet Union must be revised.
As my colleague from Parkdale-High Park said earlier in the day, and I quote: "The Government of Canada must call on the United Nations to send observers to the region and recognize the consuls of the Baltic republics in Canada."
What is happening here is clear. As the world's attention remains focused on the Persian Gulf crisis, the communist government is beating and killing people in the Baltic states. The violence and death is escalating day by day.
Military action is occurring all over this area without any shame from the communist state of Mr. Gorbachev.
I would like to quote from a January 13, 1991 press release from the Prime Minister which states: "Canada was reviewing its offers of technical assistance and new lines of credit for the purchase of foodstuffs. Further escalation would have serious consequences for Canada-U.S.S.R. relations". I believe that we should stop immediately all offers of help to the U.S.S.R.
What I have heard this last week is not of reform, not of help, and not of understanding, but rather of violence. Sending 30,000 to 40,000 additional troops to the Baltic states within the span of two or three days is totally unjustified. It will and it has already incited civil unrest.
This man has received the Nobel Peace Prize, was voted man of the year by Time magazine, and has made so much change occur in the world in six or seven years. We have seen the democratization of so many places as a result of him. He has been upstaging western politicians and leaders for many, many years. He was the man who grabbed all the attention. It is almost unbelievable that this could happen, that this man would let this happen. It is hard to believe this after we saw the Berlin wall come down, and after we saw democracy returned to areas that had not seen it for 40 and 50 years. We have seen great changes occur in his own country.
Now, in light of all this, we see the beginning of the end. Was this truly this man? Is this really this man speaking, or is it something else that I fear to even suggest could be happening?
In closing, I would like to reiterate the Liberal policy position with regard to the Baltic states. First, we never did recognize the incorporation of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania into the Union of the Soviet Socialists Republic. Second, we categorically disapprove of the forcible incorporation of the Baltic states into the U.S.S.R.
The self-determination of the people of the Baltic states must be respected by Mr. Gorbachev. Furthermore, the Soviet Union is in violation of principles seven and eight of the Helsinki Final Act. The Soviet Union must come to understand that self-determination and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms is a new world order. This has to be brought home. Mr. Gorbachev must be made to believe this. It is hard for
January 21, 1991

me to believe that after all that has happened in the last number of years that this could come about.
I want to commend all the speakers who have taken part in this debate. I want to say thank you and give the floor to my hon. colleague.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   BALTIC STATES ACTIONS OF U.S.S.R. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the House for allowing me this opportunity to talk on a very important matter.
Let me first say how proud I am of the House when it can come together unanimously, as it should more often, in terms of this issue. Unanimously we have condemned the actions of the Soviet Union in its aggression towards these three Baltic states, and parliamentarians have been able to come together in a very non-partisan way and be supportive of these three independent states. I think that is commendable.
I also want to take this opportunity to thank and congratulate the government and the Prime Minister for moving quickly to indicate to Mikhail Gorbachev that what he has done is unacceptable.
I was impressed by the speech of the right hon. secretary of state who indicated that at least Canada is moving quickly and forcefully, perhaps not as forcefully as we would like, but I will get to that in a moment, to demonstrate our willingness and our political will to ensure that the Soviet Union understands clearly a very clear message again from Canada that we will not stand for this aggression toward these three independent states.
The government can do more, along with Parliament, to ensure that the message is not lost while the world's attention is directed to a very other important region of the world, the Middle East.
I also want to thank the members from Parkdale- High Park, Scarborough Centre, and Winnipeg Transco-na, the chairpeople of the committee that seized this issue some time ago and made sure that parliamentarians were well aware of what the situation was.
I want to highlight a few points: The atrocity toward these three Baltic nations of Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia started 50 years ago. Fifty years ago that atrocity began by the U.S.S.R. when in fact it invaded, maybe not by the force that it is using today, but by the stroke of a
pen it took away the independence of those three states. To this very day, those three Baltic states have been looking to the world and to Canada to essentially stand up and say that illegal annexation by the Soviet Union of those three independent republics should not have happened, cannot happen, and we cannot remain silent anymore.
I shared the joys-as many of you did-one year ago when in fact the democratic governments were elected. We shared their joys. I was in the church basement of the Lithuanian community in London, Ontario. One could see the tears of joy from the people as they heard the votes coming in to re-establish their independence, to rededicate their independence, and we shared that joy with them.
This past Sunday I shared their horror and their anguish at what was happening again to their countries when, in fact, the Soviet Union moved in to Lithuania and Latvia, essentially killing and brutalizing those people and those countries again.
It is absolutely necessary that we collectively indicate and show our political willingness that we are serious about this matter, that the world is serious, that Mikhail Gorbachev cannot hope to hide behind the veil of what is happening in the Persian Gulf to try to go in the back door and re-establish that illegal authority in those three Baltic states.
We, as parliamentarians, supporting those people and their free and democratic spirit and their willingness to exist in peaceful coalition, hopefully with the U.S.S.R., take this opportunity of demanding that the UN take this issue seriously and that the CSCE also look at this matter in a very serious manner. Also, that we, and our government, tell the Soviet Union and the new world order that the atrocities now perpetrated on these three Baltic states again cannot be tolerated any more.
If this government really wanted to demonstrate its true commitment to the three Baltic states, it would finally recognize these three Baltic states as truly independent states. While we have never recognized the illegal annexation of these three Baltic states by the U.S.S.R., I think it is most appropriate today or tomorrow for this government, along with Parliament, to

re-establish or re-dedicate themselves to recognizing and giving full diplomatic recognition to those three Baltic republics. That would show our political will in coming to grips with this crisis.	pursuant to order made earlier this day, I declare the motion carried.
